title: Liquid metal dispersed single-atom catalyst with high-temperature stability

paper_content.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) enable greener and more economically sustainable chemical production by significantly improving thermocatalysis efficiency and selectivity through maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environments. Unfortunately, SACs are fundamentally constrained by the stability owing to the severe aggregation of single atoms, especially under the high-temperature thermocatalysis operations, which compromises the overall catalytic performance. Here, we report a synthetic strategy to realize the highly thermal-stable SACs resistance to sintering at harsh conditions through harnessing the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. A stable liquid metal-active metal interaction is formed, profiting from the superior metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal, active metal atoms can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as the metallic single-atom state at high temperatures. This catalyst exhibits outstanding thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation, sustaining stable operation for over 100 h at 650 oC with an impressive ethylene selectivity of 98%. The strategy of constructing stable metal-metal interactions by utilizing the inherent metal affinity and dynamic fluidity of liquid metal will pave a practical way for the design of highly thermal-stable SACs.
paper_content.introduction:
Industrial thermocatalysis holds great promise for improving the efficiency and sustainability of thermochemical processes and producing value-added chemicals in the modern chemical industry1–3. Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have garnered extensive attention for the development of highly efficient, sustainable, cost-effective catalysts in thermocatalysis fields due to their maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environment4–8.

However, constructing highly thermally durable SACs is a significant challenge in industrial applications. This is owing to the inherently ultra-high surface energy of single atoms, and the high temperature (> 300 oC) provides enough energy to overcome the diffusion barrier of single atoms, leading to the migration of single atoms and severe agglomeration9. In the current paradigm, it is prevalent to stabilize SACs by modulating supports (such as carbon-based supports10, metal oxides characterized by defection11–14, and so on) that tune interactions between metal atoms and supports. However, the presence of a strong bonding interaction between the supports and the single atoms may result in the compromise of the unique coordination structure of the single atoms, thereby diminishing the catalytic activity and even deactivation15,16. In terms of the strategy of using porous supports to spatially confine single atoms (such as molecular sieves and metal-organic frameworks)17,18, surmounting the substantial surface energy of the single atoms is still difficult, which will lead to inevitable aggregation of single atoms at elevated temperatures19,20. Hence, designing an optimal support that balances metal-support interaction for realizing highly efficient thermal-stable SACs remains an obstacle.

Inspired by the rule of thumb “like dissolves like”, it is promising to take advantage of unique metal-metal interaction to efficiently disperse active metals to acquire stable single atoms with inherently high metal activity by using the liquid metal as the dispersion21–23. Herein, we achieve the highly efficient dispersion of single atoms with unprecedented thermal stability by utilizing the inherent fluidity and metal affinity of liquid metal. As a demonstration, gallium (Ga), capable of an ideal liquid environment, was employed to spontaneously disperse active metal platinum (Pt). Exceptionally thermal-stable Pt single atoms dispersed by Ga that survived at 650 oC were realized. In this system, profiting from the superior metal affinity of Ga with Pt, Pt–Pt bonds are broken at elevated temperatures, and subsequently the mobile Pt atoms are captured by Ga to form the stable Pt–Ga interaction, accomplishing the highly efficient dispersion of Pt single atoms. The fluidity of liquid metal and the stable Pt–Ga interaction ensure that the Pt atoms can remain dynamically scattered throughout the whole liquid metal dispersion system. Additionally, liquid metal dispersed single atoms can self-update onto the catalysis interface continuously, promoting catalytic reactions at the interface. Hence, these liquid metal dispersed SACs manifested remarkable thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation (EDH), sustaining stable operation for over 100 hours at 650 oC with ethylene selectivity of 98%. Furthermore, the elemental composition of the system was extended to other noble metals, demonstrating the universality of the synthetic strategy. This elucidates the promising potential in realizing highly thermal-stable SACs.
paper_content.results:
The design of thermal-stable liquid metal dispersed SACs

With increasing temperature, the diffusivity of single atoms is accelerated, thereby enhancing their migration and subsequent aggregation into larger clusters or particles due to thermodynamics favoring lower total surface energy states9,24. In essence, the competition of aggregation reflected the competitive bonding between single atom/single atom and single atom/support. Establishing highly efficient as well as stable metal-support interaction is crucial for blocking the aggregation and sintering of single atoms at high temperatures. In this work, we make the realization of thermal-stable SACs by utilizing liquid metal to disperse and stabilize active metals (Fig. 1a). The abundance of metallic bonds in the liquid metal makes it an ideal medium for effectively dispersing active metals with similar metallic bonds, and the active metals can keep the metallic state. At elevated temperatures, enough energy is provided to break metallic bonds in the active metals. Furthermore, the fluidity of liquid metals drives the dispersion of active atoms in liquid metals at elevated temperatures. These dynamically migrating single atoms can be subsequently combined with liquid metal, profiting from its good metallic affinity and forming a stable interaction between these two kinds of atoms. In light of this, equipped with the naturally metallic affinity and fluidity of liquid metal, the highly thermal-stable SACs can be realized.

The liquid metal dispersed SACs are synthesized by dissolving Pt nanoparticles into liquid Ga at elevated temperatures. The mechanism illustrating the formation process of the liquid metal dispersed SACs is shown in Fig. 1a. Firstly, the Pt particles were sprinkled evenly over the liquid metal. As the temperature gradually increases, the solubility of the active metal in the dispersion is further increased, and the active metal can efficiently disperse in the liquid metal within its limited solubility. The Pt−Pt bonds in the original Pt metal nanoparticles are broken and tend to bind tightly to Ga atoms and form a thermodynamically stable configuration with Ga atoms, benefiting from the good affinity between Ga and Pt. The stable Pt−Ga interaction curtails the sintering of Pt single atoms. Moreover, according to the Arrhenius equation25, the thermal motion of atoms would be intensified by high temperature, promoting the rapid diffusion between Pt and Ga atoms and the continuous renewal of Pt single atoms exposed on the catalytic surface (Fig. 1b). In contrast, when single atoms are anchored to solid supports, their co-migration with the supports becomes kinetically constrained. Once the metal-support interactions become insufficient to compensate for the inherently high surface energy of single atoms, these atoms tend to detach from the solid supports and aggregate. This process is exothermic, where minimization of total surface energy governs particle growth26. Meanwhile, some single atoms may embed into the lattice of supports, becoming buried when the interaction between the support and metal atoms is too strong. These lead to the loss of active sites, reducing the stability of SACs and consequently affecting their activity and selectivity (Fig. 1c).

Thermal stability of active metal atoms mono-dispersed in liquid Ga

Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were employed to elucidate the atomic-scale dispersed state of active metal in liquid metal (computational details are provided in the supplementary information). Using Pt as a model of Pt cluster, we investigated the structural evolution of both clustered and dispersed Pt in liquid Ga during 10 ps simulations at 923 K (Figs. 2a, b and Supplementary Movs. 1, 2). The calculated total energy versus time curves for the Ga Pt system containing clustered Pt and dispersed Pt (Fig. 2c) reveal that the dispersed Pt generally exhibits lower total energy compared to the aggregated Pt clusters within the simulated 10 ps. The results indicate that the remarkable atomic diffusion of liquid Ga metal at high temperature promotes the migration of heterogeneous active metal atoms, thereby stabilizing their dispersed atomic state in liquid Ga.

The relatively high Pt concentration in the Ga Pt system leads to intermittent formation of Pt dimer, as evidenced by the time-dependent curve of the shortest Pt–Pt distance (Supplementary Fig. 1). To further elucidate the actual existence state of Pt atoms in liquid Ga, we performed AIMD simulations of the Ga Pt system (a Pt dimer embedded in Ga ) at 923 K. The 10 ps NVT ensemble simulations (Fig. 2d) display that the Pt–Pt interatomic distance progressively increases from 4.18 Å to 11.63 Å, significantly exceeding the Pt–Pt bond length of 2.65 ~ 2.79 Å28. This unequivocally confirms that Pt atoms preferentially exist as monatomic species in the liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Movs. 3, 4). Further statistical analysis of the coordination environment of Pt atoms in the Ga Pt system shows that the dominant coordination numbers for individual Pt atoms are 8 or 9 (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4), implying that mono-dispersed Pt atoms migrate within liquid Ga in the form of clusters such as Ga Pt or Ga Pt (Supplementary Fig. 5).

To fundamentally understand the thermodynamic preference for Pt mono-dispersion in liquid Ga, we systematically calculated the bond energy difference ∆E (∆𝐸 = 𝐸 + 𝐸̅ −2𝐸 ) only for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figs. 6 ~ 11). Here, 𝐸̅ represents the average Ga–Ga bond energy in the Ga molecular clusters, 𝐸 denotes the Pt–Pt bond energy in the (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, and 𝐸 refers to the Ga–Pt bond energy in the Ga Pt molecular clusters. The results indicate that the ∆E values for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, evaluated using different computational methods (B3LYP, MN15L, and M06L), are all greater than zero. This demonstrates that in these molecular systems, the Ga atoms involved in bond-breaking readily disrupt the Pt–Pt bonds, leading to the formation of stable Pt–Ga–Pt bridging units, thereby promoting the single-atom dispersion of Pt in liquid Ga. Meanwhile, we calculated the formation energies of Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga molecules, which were determined to be 101.1, 46.2, and 57.9 kcal mol–1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12 and Fig. 2f). Additionally, we roughly estimated the energy barriers of Ga atom insertion into the Pt–Pt bond to be 58.2, 13.4, and 40.2 kcal mol–1 by performing rigid scans of the Pt–Ga–Pt angle (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Fig. 2f). These results clearly demonstrate that, both thermodynamically and kinetically, Ga atoms in liquid Ga at 923 K can readily disrupt Pt–Pt bonds, thereby promoting the mono-dispersion of Pt atoms.

To more intuitively demonstrate the mono-dispersion state of Pt atoms in Ga, we constructed Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures with Pt contents of 2 at% and 0.2 at%, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 14). Meanwhile, based on a training dataset containing 17347 structures and a test dataset of 1926 structures, we trained a Ga–Pt neuroevolution potential model (Supplementary Fig. 15). The consistency between the calculated and experimental solubility validates the effectiveness of the constructed machine learning force field in evaluating the dissolution of Pt in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 16). Subsequently, we performed 20 ns NVT molecular dynamics simulations at 923 K on the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures using the trained Ga–Pt machine-learning potential. The simulation results clearly indicate that the Pt cluster rapidly disperse in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, we analyzed the proportions of mono-dispersed and dimerized Pt states in all structures over the last 10 ns (Fig. 2g). In the Ga Pt structure, the proportion of mono-dispersed Pt was 98.2%, while in the Ga Pt structure, it reached 99.9%. The results clearly demonstrate that in structures with Pt content of 2 at% or below, Pt atoms can be considered fully mono-dispersed at 923 K. Moreover, the calculated average numbers of surface atoms in the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures are 5.4 and 3.0, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 18 and Supplementary Fig. 19), and the temporal evolution of the vertical migration of individual Pt atoms and their probability distribution demonstrate a preferential tendency to migrate toward the surface (Supplementary Fig. 20). These indicate that a certain proportion of mono-dispersed Pt atoms can continuously exist on the liquid surface and participate in relevant catalytic reactions. Overall, the stable Ga Pt and similar clusters that are formed profited from the favorable affinity between Ga and Pt inhibit the aggregation and sintering of Pt during thermal motion, laying the foundation for synthesizing the highly thermal-stable SACs.

Characterization of liquid catalyst

To further validate that liquid metal can act as the dispersion for single atoms, we synthesized the Ga-dispersed Pt SACs (Pt SACs@Ga). The detailed structure of the catalyst was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The Pt species in the liquid metal exists in a mono-disperse distribution without the obvious occurrence of aggregated Pt (Fig. 3a). The bright-field image of Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst maintains an almost invariant brightness across the whole particle and the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) data shows no diffraction spots of Pt in the amorphous ring, revealing the lack of long-range order structure in the Ga–Pt catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Fig. 3b). Furthermore, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum was employed to reveal the chemical composition and electronic structure of the liquid metal dispersed SACs. Before the execution of XPS measurements, the sample underwent etching with argon ions to eliminate the natural oxide layer and surface contaminants. Ga 2p peaks appear at 1116.73 eV and 1116.59 eV (Fig. 3c), which are consistent with the reported binding energies of metallic Ga (Ga0 2p =1116.70 eV). Meanwhile, due to the higher electronegativity of Pt (2.28) than that of Ga (1.81)29, the Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga system served as the electron acceptor, and the Pt 4f and 4f peaks in Pt SACs@Ga exhibit a positive shift (1.0 eV) than those in pure Pt metal (Fig. 3d). It is a consensus that metallic Pt0 species occupy a preeminent role as the active sites for many catalytic processes30–32. This guarantees a proficient and robust distribution of single atoms while preserving their catalytic activity. Furthermore, the absence of the obvious aggregation of Pt atoms in the Pt SACs@Ga is further identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) tests, where no signal of Pt (PDF#04-0802) is observed (Supplementary Fig. 22). To mitigate the potential inaccuracies arising from the insensitivity of XRD to small Pt clusters, the pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was conducted to delve into the interatomic structure of the Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 23). The absence of Pt–Pt bonds indicates that Pt is distributed nearly at the atomic level within the liquid Ga without the formation of Pt clusters. These observations suggest that liquid metal can achieve the efficient uniform dispersion of highly active single atoms at elevated temperatures.

To further verify the exact dispersion state of Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga catalyst, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were conducted. The X-ray absorption edge near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum shows that the intensity of the white line at the L edge of Pt lies between that of the Pt foil and that of PtO . Correspondingly, the k -weighted R-space Fourier transformed spectra of the extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectra (EXAFS) show the prominent peak at 2.14 Å for Pt SACs@Ga distinguished from that of the Pt–O (1.62 Å) bonds for PtO and the Pt–Pt bonds (2.24 Å) for Pt foil (Fig. 3f). All these results intuitively indicate that the Pt exists in the single-atom state in liquid metal.

EDH performance of liquid metal dispersed SACs

Based on the computational results, the liquid metal dispersed SACSs theoretically feature excellent thermal stability at high temperatures. It is necessary to conduct specific high-temperature tests for verification. Pt-based catalysts are used for the dehydrogenation of alkanes due to their high efficiency in activating the C−H bonds of alkanes and low propensity in breaking C−C bonds33,34. And Pt−Sn/Al O (Oleflex process) is the primary industrial technology operated for direct propane dehydrogenation35. While it suffers from severe sintering and coke, which results in rapid deactivation and restricts the selectivity36. Therefore, as a proof of concept, the thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs was validated by EDH. As shown in Fig. 4a, when exposed to ethane, Pt single atoms exposed on the surface capture ethane molecules and synergistically activate C–H bonds, leading to selective EDH to ethylene. Meanwhile, the fluidic characteristic of liquid metal dispersed SACs at operating conditions enables continuous replenishment of catalytically active Pt atoms onto the surface. The stable interaction between Pt−Ga effectively blocks the aggregation of Pt atoms during the constant migration. Benefiting from the advantages mentioned above, these adaptive surface active sites maintain long-term activity and thermal stability.

To circumvent the issue of inadequate interaction between the liquid metal dispersed SACs and the reaction gas, the porous support is utilized to amplify the gas mass transfer rate. So, we coupled liquid metal dispersed SACs with porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) by the physical approach of ultrasonication to increase the contact surface area between the liquid metal support SACs and gas reactants. As demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 24, EDS mappings revealed a well-distribution of Ga, Si, and Al, indicating the liquid metal is uniformly loaded in the ZSM-5 zeolite framework. Upon heating, Pt will be spontaneously dispersed in Ga homogeneously, achieving the preparation of a zeolite-dispersed liquid metal supported SACs (Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5). Further, we performed in situ XRD to explore the dispersing process of Pt (Supplementary Fig. 25). The diffraction peak observed at 43 ~ 47o originates from the carbon in situ reactor (Supplementary Fig. 26). Initially, the characteristic peaks of Pt can be apparently observed, which are located at 39.76o and 46.24o. With the temperature increasing, the characteristic peaks of Pt were gradually weakened and disappeared subsequently, proving the dispersion of Pt particles.

The catalytic performance was evaluated in non-oxidative EDH at 923 K in a fixed-bed quartz U-tube reactor under atmospheric pressure with a feed gas of 12.5 vol% C H in Ar. The Pt particles/ZSM-5 catalyst, which is synthesized by direct mixing commercial Pt particles with ZSM-5, exhibits ethane conversion at 9.5% and ethylene selectivity at 82.6% (Figs. 4b, c). Interestingly, the liquid metal dispersed SACs are highly active with ethane conversion at 17.8% and ethylene selectivity at 98.3%. This is because the introduction of liquid metal alters the state of Pt. By dispersing Pt particles into single Pt atoms, the utilization of Pt atoms is maximized to achieve high conversion rates. Furthermore, since the size of Pt particle significantly influences catalytic performance, larger Pt nanoparticles typically promote C−C cleavage and deep dehydrogenation side reactions37. In contrast, Pt-based catalysts dispersed at the atomic scale exhibit excellent selectivity for ethylene due to their superior activation of C−H bonds in alkanes, while simultaneously limiting C−C bond cleavage to prevent dehydrogenation reactions. Therefore, when liquid metal is introduced, Pt exists in a single-atom state, enabling the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst to achieve high selectivity. To verify the universality of the strategy that liquid metals can disperse metals into single atoms, we extended the synthesis approach to other systems and successfully synthesized liquid metal dispersed Rh SACs (Supplementary Fig. 27). Moreover, Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 exhibits significantly improved catalytic performance compared to Rh particles/ZSM-5 in EDH (Supplementary Fig. 28).

To gain a deeper understanding of the effects of liquid metal dispersed SACs and nano catalysts on the dehydrogenation reaction of ethane, we conducted kinetic studies on both types of catalysts. We measured the ethane conversion in a temperature range of 883 ~ 933 K and fitted the data according to the Arrhenius equation to calculate the apparent activation energy for EDH. The apparent activation energies for Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 and Pt particles/ZSM-5 are 102.44 kJ mol−1 and 137.18 kJ mol−1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 29). The significantly reduced activation energy indicates a decreased energy barrier that needs to be overcome for the reaction to proceed. And the single Pt atom dispersed in the liquid Ga can more effectively weaken the C–H bond of ethane than Pt particles. Therefore, the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibits superior catalytic performance.

The performance of the liquid metal dispersed SACs in the durability test is presented in Fig. 4d. It exhibits sustainable conversion and selectivity in the continuous reaction for 100 h, where the constant ethane conversion of ~18% is obtained without attenuation. And liquid metal dispersed SACs exhibit a steady ethene productivity of around 14.3 g g −1 h−1 during the 100 h Pt EDH test. The catalyst displays no deactivation trend during the testing period, indicating a reasonable expectation of more durable stability. Notably, the XANES spectrum and R-space of liquid metal dispersed SACs after 100 h EDH at Pt L -edge are similar to those of pristine liquid SACs (Figs. 4e, f and Figs. 3e, f), demonstrating exceptional structural integrity under prolonged thermal catalysis. The catalytic performance and structural characterization together confirmed the superior thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs in extremely high temperatures, which remarkably outperforms the traditional solid support loaded SACs. To further substantiate the thermal stability performance of our work, comparing the catalytic reaction temperatures and time on stream of Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 with reported SACs (Supplementary Tab. 1), where the results remain outstanding. The excellent stability, selectivity, and conversion indicate the potential of liquid metal dispersed SACs for reactions limited in harsh conditions.
paper_content.methods:
Chemicals and materials

Gallium (Ga, 99.999%) was purchased from Shanghai Minor Metals Co. Ltd., platinum (Pt, 99.9%) and molecular sieve (ZSM-5 zeolites, Si/Al = 45) were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Inc. Rhodium (Rh, 99.95%) powder was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. High-purity ethane (99.99%) was purchased from Wuhan Xiangyun Gas Technology Co., Ltd. and was purified using 4A zeolite before reaction.

Catalyst synthesis

Synthesis of liquid metal dispersed SACs

The liquid metal dispersed SACs were synthesized by dissolving Pt or Rh nanoparticles into molten Ga in a tube furnace in a H /Ar mixture gas at 650 oC, with a heating rate of 5 oC min–1.

Synthesis of the catalyst for EDH

In order to increase the mass transfer of the ethane, the liquid metal is coupled with the ZSM-5 (Ga/ZSM-5) by sonication as follows. The liquid Ga and ZSM-5 zeolites were transferred to ethylene glycol, and the solution was sonicated by a probe-type sonicator for 2 h (5 s on and 3 s off) at a power of 290 W. After sonication, the resultant precipitations were washed with ethanol and water 3 times. And then the resultant was flash frozen in liquid nitrogen for five minutes and freeze-dried at −40 oC, under a pressure less than 200 mTorr, for 24 h using the FreeZone 4.5 Liter Benchtop Freeze Dry System. The Pt particles were mixed with Ga/ZSM-5 (or pure ZSM-5) and heated from room temperature to 650 oC at a rate of 10 oC min–1 in the reactor under a H /Ar mixed gas atmosphere. The mixture was then held at 650 oC for 30 minutes to complete the synthesis of the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst (or Pt particles/ZSM-5). The Pt : Ga atomic ratio of the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst prepared for catalytic testing was maintained at 0.2 : 99.8. After purging the H from the U-tube, the catalyst was ready for catalytic testing. Similarly, replace the Pt particles with Rh particles and undergo the same treatment to obtain Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 (or Rh particles/ZSM-5), and the Rh : Ga atomic ratio of the Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst used for catalytic testing is also maintained at 0.2 : 99.8.

Catalyst characterizations

The morphology of the liquid metal dispersed SACs was characterized by an F200 transmission electron microscope (TEM) (JEOL, Japan) operated at 200 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) data was employed by PANalytical X’Pert-Pro diffractometer, with a Cu K𝛼 radiation (𝜆 = 0.15406 nm), in the 2θ scan mode ranging from 10o to 80o at a scan speed of 8o min−1. In situ XRD was collected with the Rigaku Ultima Ⅳ instrument using Cu Kα (λ = 1.5406 Å) radiation at 40 kV and 40 mA, and the operating voltage and current were 40 kV and 40 mA, respectively. The catalysts were scanned at a rate of 8o min−1 in the 2θ range of 35o ~ 60o. Pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was performed at room temperature in an air atmosphere by SmartLab, with a Ag K𝛼 radiation (𝜆 = 0.056088 nm). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were taken on a high-resolution Thermo Fisher Scientific ESCALAB Xi+ spectrometer using Al K𝛼 radiation under vacuum. Pt L and Rh K edge XAFS spectra were collected at the BL11B beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). During the measurement, the synchrotron radiation ring was operated at 3.5 GeV, and the electron current was 200 mA in the top-up mode. The samples were sealed in Kapton film. For the measurement of Pt L edge, the white light was monochromatized by a Si (111) double-crystal monochromator. And the white light was monochromatized by a Si (311) double-crystal monochromator when the Rh K edge was measured. The corresponding metal foils were used as a reference sample to calibrate and measure in the transmission mode. All XAFS spectra were processed using the IFEFFIT package. The elemental composition of the samples before and after the reaction was determined by inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES).

Catalytic performance and kinetic behavior measurements

EDH tests were performed under atmospheric pressure in a fixed-bed quartz U-tube reactor. Catalysts were weighed and loaded into 10 mm outside diameter, 8 mm interior diameter U-tube reactor. 5 sccm of argon and 15 sccm of hydrogen were flowed at 650 oC for 10 minutes to reduce any metal oxides. And then the reactor was purged with 20 sccm argon for 5 min to prevent hydrogen residue. The EDH reaction was conducted in a C H /Ar mixture gas (Vol C H /Vol Ar = 1:7) with a flow rate of 20 mL min−1. The outlet gas products were observed by an online mass spectrometer (Pro-tech, PM-QMS, China ). The conversion of ethane and selectivity to all carbonaceous products (including coke) were calculated as follows:

Ethane conversion = (molar flow rate of carbon (C) in products / molar flow rate of total C in effluent (C H +products)) * 100% (1)

Product selectivity = (molar flow rate of C in product i / molar flow rate of C in all products) * 100% (2)

The kinetic behavior of the catalyst for EDH needs to minimize transport limitations. Therefore, the conversion was limited to 5 ~ 15% while ethylene selectivity remained above 90% by systematically varying the catalyst amount. By analyzing the temperature and pressure dependence of these rates, we extracted the activation energy and reaction order for the reaction.

Theoretical calculations

Quantum chemistry calculations and Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations

To investigate the atomic-level dispersion of active metals in the liquid Ga, we initially constructed a Ga Pt cubic cell model using LAMMPS-17Apr2024 software. The initial cell parameter was set to 13 Å, with Pt as a cluster molecule and the remaining 90 Ga atoms randomly distributed. Subsequently, ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP.5.4.4) to the potential energy curves for both clustered and dispersed states of Pt in the Ga Pt structural model at 923 K. For the dispersed state, the damping coefficients for Ga and Pt were set to 10 and 5, respectively, while for the clustered state, they were set to 10 and 1000. All calculations were conducted using the GGA-PBEsol functional38 and employed the Langevin thermostat and ParrinIello-Rahman method39,40 for the isothermal-isobaric (nP T) ensemble. The cutoff energy was set to 400 eV with an energy convergence tolerance of 10–6 eV, and the simulation time was 10 ps. Due to the relatively high Pt content in the Ga Pt system, occasional Pt units were observed in the simulation results. Therefore, we further performed similar ab initio molecular dynamics simulations for the Ga Pt system, and an extra 10 ps NVT MD simulation was carried out starting from the last snapshot of the NPT simulation. Additionally, the crystalNN statistical method41 was used to evaluate the Pt–Pt bonding in liquid Ga. To gain further insight into the dispersion of Pt atoms in liquid Ga, we employed the B3LYP/LANL2DZ, MN15L/LANL2DZ42 and M06L/LANL2DZ methods to calculate the bond energy difference ∆E . The specific calculation method of ∆E for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters is based on Equation (3):

∆𝐸 = 𝐸 + 𝐸̅ −2𝐸 (3)

Here, 𝐸̅ represents the average Ga–Ga bond energy in the Ga molecular clusters, 𝐸 denotes the Pt–Pt bond energy in the (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, and 𝐸 refers to the Ga–Pt bond energy in the Ga Pt molecular clusters. All bond energy calculations were corrected for basis set superposition error (BSSE). Furthermore, we constructed cluster structures such as Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga, optimizing all cluster molecules using the B3LYP/LANL2DZ method. Additionally, we performed rigid scans of the PtGaPt angle in the Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga cluster systems to roughly estimate the energy barrier associated with the incorporation of Ga atoms into the Pt–Pt bond.

Ga–Pt machine learning force field training and molecular dynamics simulations

We constructed a dataset for the Ga–Pt binary system, comprising 17347 training structures and 1926 test structures. These structures cover bulk and surface structures of α-Ga, β-Ga, γ-Ga, Pt, Ga Pt, Ga Pt, Ga Pt , Ga Pt and Ga Pt , Ga–Pt bulk structures with varying compositions (Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , and Ga Pt ). Nanoparticle systems such as Pt , Pt , Pt , and Pt were also considered. The dataset was initially generated using isothermal–isobaric (NPT) Ab initio molecular dynamics (MD) simulations under ambient pressure (0.0001 GPa) and temperatures ranging from 0 to 9000 K. A machine learning potential was trained using data from AIMD simulations.

Density functional theory calculations

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The calculations employed a plane-wave basis set with the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method and standard pseudo-potentials for Ga and Pt. The GGA-PBE sol density functional was selected, along with D3 dispersion interaction corrections. All calculations were conducted in high-precision mode (PREC = Accurate), with a plane-wave cutoff energy set to 400 eV and without symmetry constraints (ISYM = 0). To ensure accuracy, the electronic self-consistent loop converged to a tolerance of 10–6 eV (EDIFF = 1.0E–6). The Methfessel-Paxton first-order smearing method (ISMEAR = 1) was applied. The conjugate gradient algorithm was used for electronic minimization, and the maximum number of steps for electronic self-consistent (SCF) cycles was set to 999. A k-point mesh was automatically generated based on the reciprocal lattice vectors of the unit cell, with a k-point spacing of approximately 0.040 Å–1 in each direction. Only single-point calculations were performed, as the DFT computations were primarily used to generate labels for training data.

Machine learning force field training

The training of the force field is performed using the efficient Neural Evolutionary Potential (NEP) method and the GPUMD code. The training dataset is sourced from the previously completed PBE -D3 calculations. The cutoff radii for the radial and angular descriptors are set to 8 Å and 6 Å, respectively. The weights for energy, force, and virial stress are 1.0, 1.0, and 0.1, respectively. The number of neurons in the hidden layer of the neural network (NN) is 50. The NEP potential function underwent 200,000 optimization iterations over the entire training set. The final results include the root mean square errors (RMSE) of energy and atomic forces.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The work by Ziyue Zeng's and coworkers deals with a very relevant topic in the field of catalysis. The paper is well written and contains relevant information. However, the paper is not suitable for Nature Communications and needs to be fundamentally revised in order to be suitable for a more specialised journal in the future. The reason is simple: the main claims of the article, namely that a single Pt atom can be stabilised in liquid gallium to perform high-temperature dehydrogenation catalysis in the form of supported liquid metal catalysis, are by no means new, but have already been published (with slightly different terminology) in more than 50 articles (this reviewer has verified this today using SCOPUS), including high-ranking publications in Nature Chemistry, such as the work by Rahim et al. in Nature Chemistry, Volume 14, 935-941 from 2022. (DOI: 10.1038/s41557-022-00965-6).
Even the idea to immobilize liquid Ga-Pt alloy droplets on porous supports for alkane dehydrogenation reactions is far from new. Under the name ‘Supported Catalytically Active Liquid Metal Solutions (SCALMS)’ (Nature Chemistry, 2017, 9(9), 862-867, DOI: 10.1038/nchem.2822, and paper citing this work) more than 30 paper have been published describing exactly this concept, 11 of these deal with Ga-Pt systems including preparation by ultrasonication and theoretical calculations to prove the isolated nature of Pt in Ga. Seven of these papers deal with propane dehydrogenation which is a very similar reaction to ethane hydrogenation.
In this light, this reviewer finds it striking that none of these earlier works were cited by Ziyue Zeng and coworkers. This is strange – and even if one takes into account the slightly different terminology used in the various articles – a proper and rigorous approach could have led to the conclusion that the work described in the current submission lacks the required novelty for a publication in Nature Communications.
In conclusion, this reviewer recommends studying the existing literature much more carefully and then publishing some of the interesting detailed information in the submitted manuscript in a much more specialised journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript, the authors described a strategy to realize the highly thermal-stable single-atom catalysts (SACs) resistance to sintering through harnessing the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. This work provides a novel approach for addressing the thermal instability of SACs under high-temperature conditions, which is regarded as the most critical and persistent challenge in single-atom catalysis. The proposed liquid metal-dispersed SACs exhibited outstanding thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation, sustaining stable operation for over 100 h at 650 oC with an impressive ethylene selectivity of 98%. This work not only resolves a key limitation in SACs but also paves the avenue to practical deployment of SACs for practical industrial thermocatalysis.
Hence, I would like to recommend the publication in Nature Communications. The following are several minor details for the authors to consider:
1. It is very interesting to use liquid metal with dynamic fluidity and metallicity to stabilize the single atoms. How can a single atom be "anchored" on this dynamically renewed surface? Is this anchoring a static "locking" or a dynamic "stabilization" that relies on the rapid dynamic reconfiguration of the liquid metal surface? I'd be very glad to hear some explanations or assumptions.
2. As demonstrated in page 8 line 6, the Pt−Pt bond length is 2.65~2.79 Å. However, in Figure 2d, the authors drew a gray area between 2.65~3.35 Å. Does the grey area represent the inherent bond length of Pt−Pt, or is there any specific basis or standard for this range?
3. In Figure 2f, the potential energy of Pt–Pt (107.9 kcal/mol) is lower than that of Ga–Pt and Ga–Ga. I wonder whether this is in contradiction to the opinion that Pt tends to form Ga–Pt bonds within liquid metal.
4. Pt is regarded as a good catalyst for ethane dehydrogenation. I am very curious whether Ga and porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) will have any impact on the conversion and selectivity of the ethane dehydrogenation reaction. Ga/ZSM-5 was also proposed effective for dehydrogenation of alkanes(eg. DOI:10.1016/j.jcat.2024.115834; 10.1021/acscatal.7b04295, etc.). It would be better for the authors to elaborate on the catalytic performances of Pt/ZSM-5 and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5.
5. The authors have demonstrated the unique advantages of liquid metal in dispersing single atoms and maintaining their high-temperature stability. I am curious whether liquid metal has any advantages over the solid carriers for synthesizing SACs. Please give corresponding explanations.
6. A few specific minor errors:
1) Redefining abbreviations: The authors have already defined the single-atom catalysts and given the abbreviation in line 2 of the abstract, but it is abbreviated again in line 5.
2) Spelling mistake: in Supplementary Fig. 1, the word “luctuates” may be misspelled.
3) Other error: in Supplementary Fig. 11, the x-coordinate is incorrect.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This work reports liquid metal dispersed single-atom catalyst by dissolving Pt into molten Ga. In fact, it is the Pt-Ga nanoalloy in previous work. I cannot make sure this kind of nanoalloy with dissolving Pt into molten Ga is the single-atom catalyst. I donot agree with the definition of molten nanoalloy as liquid metal dispersed single-atom catalyst. Thus, I donot think this work should be published in Nature Communications. Other Comments:
1) I suggest the authors to make sure the definition of single-atom catalyst. This kind of molten Pt-Ga nanoalloy is not new, and their catalytic mechanism is the contribution of both Pt and Ga. It is NOT the case of single-atom catalyst.
2) The mechanism of high temperature stability is not clear. The authors need to prepare a single Pt atom in molten Ga, and Pt almost remain the top of the molten Ga cluster and also high temperature stability.
3) The data analysis for liquid metal dispersed single-atom catalyst is not enough for understanding high temperature stability. How to certify that the Pt atoms donot form dimer and trimer inside the molten Ga after long-time high temperature test?

reviewer considered that it has been reported. We would like to clarify.
Our work focuses on the severe sintering limitation of SACs at high temperatures
in industrial catalysis. By leveraging the fluidity and metal affinity of liquid metal, we
realized the ultra-stable SACs at 650 oC. It is worth noting that the high temperature
contributes to the dispersion of single atoms in our work rather than the agglomeration
sintering phenomenon in reported works, which is of great significance for promoting the
industrial application of SACs. The significance of our work lays as follows:
i) The realization of highly thermal-stable SACs for industrial catalysis. SACs have
emerged as promising candidates to replace conventional industrial catalysts owing to their
exceptional catalytic activity and atomic efficiency. The high surface energy of single atoms
renders them prone to migration and subsequent sintering during catalytic processes,
especially at high temperatures. Thus, it remains a formidable obstacle to developing
novel catalysts with high-temperature thermal stability. We realized the highly thermal-
stable SACs resistance to sintering at harsh conditions through harnessing the inherent metal
affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. We believe this is a crucial step forward in promoting
the application of SACs in high-temperature industrial catalysis.
ii）A brand-new strategy for achieving highly thermal-stable SACs resistance to
sintering by liquid metals. The monodispersion of Pt in liquid metals rather than
agglomeration at high temperatures is a thermodynamically favorable process, which is
owing to the selective breaking and formation of chemical bonds profiting from the inherent
metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal, active metal atoms
can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as the metallic single-atom state at high
temperatures. We have provided robust evidence for clarifying the mechanism.
Regarding the work by Rahim et al. in Nature Chemistry, Volume 14, 935–941 from
2022 (DOI: 10.1038/s41557-022-00965-6), we acknowledge that this work did indeed
disperse ~0.0001 at% Pt in liquid metal and applied it to the reactions that are limited at

tetramethylbenzidine, the reduction of methylene blue, and the electrochemical oxidation
of CH OH. However, this article (Nat. Chem. 2022, 14, 935) does not suggest that liquid

Therefore, the core innovation of work and the previously reported works are

2) As for immobilizing liquid Ga–Pt alloy droplets on porous supports, it has no
relationship with the core innovation of our work. The focus in this work is to utilize
liquid metal to address the bottleneck of agglomeration of SACs.
Firstly, the adoption of porous support is to reveal the thermal-stability essence for
the SACs dispersed by liquid metals while eliminating the influence of mass transfer.
Porous support is a commonly used strategy to enhance the mass transfer, as it guarantees a
relatively chemical inertness and the absence of mass-transfer restrictions because of the

lies in the catalytic performance of the Ga–Pt alloy itself. The work (Nat. Chem. 2017, 9,

for 100 h, substantially outperforming the referenced work. Furthermore, we have

mechanism of the excellent thermal stability of the catalyst. And for large-scale industrial
catalysis, the high cost of Pt significantly constrains large-scale applications. While existing

Comment 1: It is very interesting to use liquid metal with dynamic fluidity and
metallicity to stabilize the single atoms. How can a single atom be "anchored" on this
dynamically renewed surface? Is this anchoring a static "locking" or a dynamic
"stabilization" that relies on the rapid dynamic reconfiguration of the liquid metal surface?
I'd be very glad to hear some explanations or assumptions.
Author reply: Thank you for your valuable comment. The anchoring of single atoms
(Pt) in liquid metals fundamentally relies on a dynamic equilibrium between fluidity and
stability, achieved through the synergistic interplay of stable metal bonds and surface
reconfiguration. Profiting from the superior metal affinity of Ga with Pt, Pt–Pt bonds are
broken at elevated temperatures, and subsequently the mobile Pt atoms are captured by Ga
to form a stable Pt–Ga interaction, accomplishing the highly efficient dispersion of Pt single
atoms. The fluidity of liquid metal and the stable Pt–Ga interaction ensure that the Pt atoms
can remain dynamically scattered throughout the whole liquid metal dispersion system.
To further validate the stability mechanism of Pt single atoms dispersed in Ga, we
constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁ slab model. AIMD simulations were conducted to investigate the
motion trajectory of a single Pt atom in molten Ga (analyzing its vertical distance to the
surface). Throughout the 10 ps simulation period, a single Pt atom migrates relatively freely
within molten Ga, with a depth from the Ga surface ranging from 0 to 4.84 Å (Fig. R2).
Statistical analysis indicates a surface exposure probability of 56.3% for the isolated Pt atom.
Furthermore, considering the susceptibility of metallic Ga to oxidation state, even under
reducing atmospheres (e.g., H₂) at 923 K, a thin Ga₂O₃ layer may persist. To eliminate the
influence of Ga oxidation on Pt exposure, we also constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁O₁₀ slab model
incorporating a small number of oxygen atoms and performed a 10 ps AIMD simulation.
The simulation results demonstrate that limited oxygen atoms form Ga₂O₃ clusters with
surface Ga atoms. Under the influence of these Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga surface, the
Pt atom primarily remains within the surface and subsurface regions, exhibiting a depth
range of 0 to 2.97 Å (Fig. R2). Notably, the surface exposure probability of the single Pt
atom increases significantly to 81.3%. The single Pt atom in liquid metal migrates freely as
Ga₈Pt or Ga₉Pt clusters, retaining a finite probability of surface exposure. Crucially, the
presence of Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga surface dramatically enhances the probability
of single Pt atom surface exposure. This indicates that the Pt single atom can be stabilized
to the molten Ga surface at 923 K over extended periods, thereby serving as active sites
for the catalytic activation of C₂H₆ molecules.
Fig. R2 | The calculated curve of the distance between a single Pt atom and the surface Ga layer as
a function of time. Here, surface Ga atoms are characterized as top-layer Ga atoms in each frame
structure whose coordination number is two less than the maximum coordination number, with the zero
point in the z-direction defined as the average of the maximum and minimum z-coordinates of these
surface Ga atoms. Furthermore, the z-coordinate threshold for identifying exposed Pt atoms is defined as
the vertical distance corresponding to the closest packing radius of Re atoms relative to this zero reference
point.
Therefore, the anchoring of a single atom does not rely on static “rigid locking” but is a
dynamic process.
Comment 2: As demonstrated in page 8 line 6, the Pt−Pt bond length is 2.65~2.79 Å. However, in Figure 2d, the authors drew a gray area between 2.65~3.35 Å. Does the grey
area represent the inherent bond length of Pt−Pt, or is there any specific basis or standard
for this range?
Author reply: Thank you for your kind reminding. The gray area is marked to display
the range of bond length fluctuation during bonding between two Pt atoms. Beyond this
threshold, the Pt−Pt bond is considered dissociated, with the atoms existing in a single-atom
state. The intrinsic bond length of Pt–Pt fluctuates between 2.65 and 2.79 Å (J. Am. Chem.
Soc., 1978, 100, 2074−2079). And generally, when the distance between the two atoms is
less than 1.2 times (2.79 Å×1.2=3.35 Å) of the sum of their Cambridge Structural Database
(CSD) covalent radii, it can be considered that no chemical bond has been formed between
these two atoms and they can be regarded as independent of each other (J. Comput. Chem.,
2011, 33, 580; J. Chem. Phys., 2024, 161, 082503). Thus, the gray area spanning from 2.65
to 3.35 Å was considered to be the distance of the Pt–Pt bond. And we have clarified this
point in our revised manuscript in Figure 2 (Supplementary Information).
Comment 3: In Figure 2f, the potential energy of Pt–Pt (107.9 kcal/mol) is lower than
that of Ga–Pt and Ga–Ga. I wonder whether this is in contradiction to the opinion that Pt
tends to form Ga–Pt bonds within liquid metal.
Author reply: Thank you for your kind reminding. As you put forward, the potential
energy of Pt–Pt (107.9 kcal/mol) is lower than that of Ga–Pt (74.9 kcal/mol) and Ga–Ga
(32.5 kcal/mol) (Fig. R3). However, the dispersion of Pt in liquid metal Ga involves two
processes, including the breaking of the Pt–Pt bond and the Ga–Ga bond, and the formation
of two Ga–Pt bonds (149.8 kcal/mol). This is an exothermic process (9.4 kcal/mol).
Moreover, the Ga–Ga bond in liquid Ga is weaker than that in Ga₂ molecules. Therefore,
the breaking of Pt–Pt bonds to form Ga–Pt bonds is more favorable thermodynamically,
which is consistent with the perspective that Pt readily forms Ga–Pt bonds in liquid metal
Ga. The energetic advantage accompanied by the good affinity between Ga and Pt enables
Ga atoms to disrupt Pt–Pt bonds to form stable Pt–Ga–Pt bridging units. We also provided
a detailed elaboration on this matter from the perspectives of thermodynamics and kinetics
in the manuscript.
Fig. R3 | The calculated potential energy curves of three diatomic systems: Ga , GaPt, and Pt .
2 2
Comment 4: Pt is regarded as a good catalyst for ethane dehydrogenation. I am very
curious whether Ga and porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) will have any impact on the conversion
and selectivity of the ethane dehydrogenation reaction. Ga/ZSM-5 was also proposed
effective for dehydrogenation of alkanes (eg. DOI:10.1016/j.jcat.2024.115834;
10.1021/acscatal.7b04295, etc.). It would be better for the authors to elaborate on the
catalytic performances of Pt/ZSM-5 and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5.
Author reply: Thank you for your kind reminding. In our work, Ga was adopted as the
dispersion to achieve atomic dispersion of the active metal. This ensures a highly uniform
coordination environment of Pt atoms, which contributes to the selectivity and durability
of the SACs. The introduction of zeolite is a commonly used strategy to enhance mass
transfer. The adoption of Porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) is to reveal the thermal-stability
essence for the SACs dispersed by liquid metals while eliminating the influence of mass
transfer. We have supplemented the catalytic performance data of Pt/ZSM-5 and
Pt@Ga/ZSM-5 to clarify the roles of the liquid metal and ZSM-5, hoping to address your
questions.
1) Ga facilitates the atomic dispersion of active metals, and the highly uniform and stable
coordination environment of active centers underpins the exceptional selectivity and
durability of the SACs. Pt is recognized as an effective catalyst for alkane dehydrogenation
(Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409556). However, its catalytic activity varies
significantly across different particle sizes with a varied coordination environment of each
Pt atom (ACS Catal. 2025, 15, 12420; ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 9279). When used directly in
alkane dehydrogenation, this anisotropy promotes side reactions and reduces overall
selectivity. By dispersing Pt as single atoms onto Ga, a highly uniform coordination
environment is established, which ensures superior catalytic selectivity. Besides, the
catalytic performances of Pt/ZSM-5 and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5 were investigated to further
demonstrate the role of liquid metal in enhancing catalytic performance. As shown in Fig.
R4, benefiting from the introduction of Ga, the reaction conversion of ethane is increased
from 10% to 18%, while the selectivity of ethylene is improved from 82% to 98%.
Fig. R4 | Ethane dehydrogenation performance of Pt/ZSM-5 and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5.
2) The molecular sieve itself exhibits negligible catalytic activity, with a selectivity of
only 85% (Fig. R5). Its incorporation is intended to enhance gas-catalyst contact and
improve mass transfer efficiency.
Fig. R5 | Ethane dehydrogenation performance of pure ZSM-5 and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5.
Comment 5: The authors have demonstrated the unique advantages of liquid metal in
dispersing single atoms and maintaining their high-temperature stability. I am curious
whether liquid metal has any advantages over the solid carriers for synthesizing SACs.
Please give corresponding explanations.
Author reply: Thank you for your constructive comment. The traditional synthesis
strategies of SACs mainly contain impregnation method (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147,
32729), mass-selected soft-landing method (ACS Nano 2020, 14, 13279), coprecipitation
method (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 18737), atomic layer deposition strategy (Nature
2025, 640, 668), the host-guest strategy (Nat. Chem. 2020, 12, 764), photochemical
synthesis (Science 2016, 352, 797), etc. In most of these methods, metal precursors (such as
metal nitrates, metal chlorides, and metal acetylacetonates) are selected as the starting
materials and subjected to heat treatment or light irradiation to deconstruct the original
structure (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 18155). Traditional synthesis methods of SACs
require intricate procedures, including impregnation, aging, multiple drying cycles,
temperature-controlled thermal treatment, and acid washing purification. These processes
are not only lengthy but also involve multiple sensitive variables (e.g., pH, temperature,
heating rate), posing significant challenges to reproducibility. Furthermore, these methods
usually cannot be simply extrapolated to other systems due to their high dependence on
metal-support interactions.
The advantages of liquid metal for synthesizing SACs are as follows:
1) The convenience and highly reproducible ability. The conventional synthesis
strategies necessitate precise sequential control over impregnation, drying, pyrolysis, and
acid washing. In contrast, the liquid metal strategy requires only physical mixing of active
metal precursors (e.g., nanoparticles or even foils) with low-melting-point liquid metals
(e.g., gallium, indium), followed by heating above the melting point under an inert
atmosphere. Active metals spontaneously dissolve and disperse into single atoms within the
liquid metal dispersion, eliminating all intermediate processing steps.
2) Excellent universality. Traditional synthesis approaches suffer inherent limitations
due to their reliance on metal-support interactions, which cannot be simply extrapolated to
other systems. Typically, one approach is only applicable to specific metal-support
combinations (e.g., Pt on TiO₂, Fe on N-C), necessitating extensive screening efforts to
develop new systems (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202405017). However, since liquid
metals and most metals possess good affinity, our strategy exhibits near-universal
applicability. And driven by thermodynamics (the negative mixing entropy), any target
metal can be dispersed as single atoms in the liquid metal.
3) Near-100% atomic utilization efficiency for the active metal. Conventional
synthesis routes incur active metal loss during high-temperature precursor volatilization and
acid-washing purification. In our method, the dissolution of active metal within the liquid
metal suppresses volatilization, while the synthesis itself constitutes a purification process,
entirely eliminating acid-washing steps required to remove nanoparticles in traditional
methods. Consequently, virtually all introduced active metal atoms convert to utilizable
single-atom sites.
4) Highly uniform active site microenvironments enable precisely tunable catalytic
performance. On conventional solid supports (e.g., porous carbon, metal oxides),
anchoring sites (vacancies, doped N atoms, surface hydroxyl groups) exhibit inherent
heterogeneity in size, electronegativity, and spatial geometry. Therefore, the generated
single-atom active sites do not have a single structure, and their catalytic activity and
selectivity will be weakened, making it difficult to conduct precise structure-activity
relationship studies. Conversely, the homogeneous bulk environment of liquid metals
ensures a highly uniform coordination geometry for every active-metal atom, thereby
guaranteeing high selectivity in subsequent catalytic processes. Liquid metal provides an
ideal platform for atomic-level catalytic design and modulation.
Comment 6: A few specific minor errors: 1) Redefining abbreviations: the authors have
already defined the single-atom catalysts and given the abbreviation in line 2 of the abstract,
but it is abbreviated again in line 5. 2) Spelling mistake: in Supplementary Fig. 1, the word
“luctuates” may be misspelled. 3) Other error: in Supplementary Fig. 11, the x-coordinate
is incorrect.

Initially, the characteristic peaks of Pt can be apparently observed, which are located at 39.8o and 46.3o.
With the temperature increasing, the characteristic peaks of Pt were gradually weakened and disappeared
subsequently, proving the dispersion of Pt particles.
Finally, we thank the reviewer’s suggestion to make our manuscript more rigorous, and

readers. Please find our revisions marked in the red copy of the revised manuscript.

Author reply: Thank you for your kind reminding. The catalyst proposed in our
manuscript can be classified as a single-atom alloy (SAA) catalyst, which is a kind of SACs.
To clarify the rationale for categorizing our catalyst, we combined the definition of catalysts
and their structural characteristics to illustrate. We have carefully checked the references to
clarify the definitions of alloy, nanoalloy, single-atom catalysts (SACs), and single-atom
alloys (SAAs). Besides, the experimental characterization evidence was also provided to

1) Firstly, the catalyst proposed in our work conforms to the core definition of the
single-atom alloy catalysts that fall within the category of SACs. We systematically
analyzed the fundamental distinctions between alloys, nanoalloys, SACs, and SAAs to
address reviewers’ concerns (Fig. R6). Alloy catalysts have a long history and have been
developing over nearly 100 years (J. Chem. Educ. 1929, 6, 2097). Building upon the
classical definition wherein alloys are most conveniently defined as a metallic system
containing two or more components, irrespective of their intimacy of mixing or precise
manner of mixing (V. Ponec, G.C. Bond, Catalysis by Metals and Alloys, Elsevier,
Amsrerdam, 1995; Applied Catalysis A: General 2001, 222, 31). When the size of the alloy

1) Theoretical calculations have proved that a single Pt atom in molten Ga can
freely migrate in the molten Ga, and there is a certain probability for it being exposed
on the Ga surface. To validate this mechanism, we constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁ slab model. AIMD
simulations were conducted to investigate the motion trajectory of a single Pt atom in molten
Ga (analyzing its vertical distance to the surface). Throughout the 10 ps simulation period,
a single Pt atom migrates relatively freely within molten Ga, with a depth from the Ga
surface ranging from 0 to 4.84 Å (Fig. R7). Statistical analysis indicates a surface exposure
probability of 56.3% for the isolated Pt atom. Furthermore, considering the susceptibility of
metallic Ga to oxidation state, even under reducing atmospheres (e.g., H₂) at 923 K, a thin
Ga₂O₃ layer may persist. To eliminate the influence of Ga oxidation on Pt exposure, we also
constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁O₁₀ slab model incorporating a small number of oxygen atoms and
performed a 10 ps AIMD simulation. The simulation results demonstrate that limited
oxygen atoms form Ga₂O₃ clusters with surface Ga atoms. Under the influence of these
Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga surface, the Pt atom primarily remains within the surface
and subsurface regions, exhibiting a depth range of 0 to 2.97 Å (Fig. R10). Notably, the
surface exposure probability of the single Pt atom increases significantly to 81.3%. The
single Pt atom in liquid metal migrates freely as Ga₈Pt or Ga₉Pt clusters, retaining a finite
probability of surface exposure. Crucially, the presence of Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga
surface dramatically enhances the probability of single Pt atom surface exposure. This
indicates that the Pt single atom can be stabilized to the molten Ga surface at 923 K
over extended periods, thereby serving as active sites for the catalytic activation of
C₂H₆ molecules.

Acc. Chem. Res. 2013, 46, 1720; Nat. Catal. 2021, 4, 469; Nat. Catal. 2025, 8, 1038), it
is worth noting that the high temperature contributes to the dispersion single atoms
profited from the affinity between Ga and Pt in our work. Besides, the Pt–Ga catalyst
in our work is exactly a kind of SACs. Regarding your question, we have made a point-
by-point response, hoping to clear up your doubts.
1) As for the definition of molten nanoalloy is not liquid metal dispersed SAC,
we would like to clarify. The catalyst proposed in our work aligns with the established
definition of single-atom alloy catalysts (SAAs), which is a kind of SACs. And this has
been evidenced by both theoretical calculations and experiments.
The Pt–Ga catalyst in our work conforms to the core definition of SACs. The
concept of “SACs” was first proposed by Zhang, Li, Liu, and co-workers in 2011, in
which isolated single atoms were anchored onto nano-crystallites (Nat. Chem. 2011, 3,
634). Up to now, the SACs are universally regarded as “one kind of supported metal
catalyst with isolated metal atom sites, where the core metal atoms in the active sites are
not closely connected but interact with support” (Acc. Chem. Res. 2025, 58, 1878). The
concept of “SAAs” was first put forward in 2012 by Georgios Kyriakou et al. with two
key characteristics, which fall within the category of SACs (Science 2012, 335, 1209).
“Two key characteristics of SAAs are (i) the more active of the two components is present
in the surface of the host metal at very low concentrations [~0.01 monolayer (ML)] and
(ii) atoms of the more active component are thermodynamically more stable when
surrounded by the host metal such that no dimers or trimers are present at low coverage.”
Currently, it is commonly accepted that SAAs are a class of single-site catalysts in which
small amounts of isolated metal atoms are present in the surface layer of a metal host.
Typically, they are comprised of single atoms of a catalytically active metal alloyed into
the surface of a less reactive host metal (Chem. Rev. 2020, 120, 12044). Based on these
criteria, we conducted a rigorous comparison between the catalyst in our work and the
definition of SAAs, confirming that the catalyst in our work fully satisfies the
requirements: (a) The Pt atoms are presented as the single-atom state within Ga and
dynamically migrate onto the surface to parcipate in the catalytic reaction (which
was proved theoretically and in experiment); and (b) the Pt atoms are mainly active
centers (which was evidenced by the experiments). The detailed analysis is as follows:

theoretical calculation, machine learning, and experiments.

Our work focuses on the severe sintering limitation of SACs at high
temperatures in industrial catalysis. By leveraging the fluidity and metal affinity of
liquid metal, we realized the ultra-stable SACs at 650 oC. It is worth noting that the
high temperature contributes to the dispersion of single atoms in our work rather than the
agglomeration sintering phenomenon in reported works, which is of great significance for
promoting the industrial application of SACs. The significance of our work lies as follows:
i) The realization of highly thermal-stable SACs for industrial catalysis. SACs
have emerged as promising candidates to replace conventional industrial catalysts owing
to their exceptional catalytic activity and atomic efficiency. The high surface energy of
single atoms renders them prone to migration and subsequent sintering during catalytic
processes, especially at high temperatures. Thus, it remains a formidable obstacle to
developing novel catalysts with high-temperature thermal stability. We realized the
highly thermal-stable SACs resistance to sintering at harsh conditions through harnessing
the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal (Fig. R7). We believe this is a
crucial step forward in promoting the application of SACs in high-temperature industrial
catalysis.

ii) A brand-new strategy for achieving highly thermal-stable SACs resistance
to sintering by liquid metals. The mono-dispersion of Pt in liquid metals rather than
agglomeration at high temperatures is a thermodynamically favourable process, which is
owing to the selective breaking and formation of chemical bonds profiting from the
inherent metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal, active
metal atoms can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as the metallic single-atom
state at high temperatures. We have provided robust evidence for clarifying the
mechanism (Figure 2 and Supplementary Mov. S1 and S2 in our revised manuscript).
Besides, X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) analysis provides unequivocal proof to
verify the single-atom state of Pt in Ga before and after the ethane dehydrogenation (Fig.
R5).
Regarding the doubts about the reported works, we have conducted a
comprehensive literature search, retrieving studies on liquid metal Ga and Pt for
dehydrogenation catalysis. Previous reports focus on the catalytic performance of the Pt
in liquid metal limited in low-temperature or the catalytic performance of the alloy state
in thermal catalysis (Nat. Chem. 2022, 14, 935; ACS Appl. Nano Mater. 2024, 7, 24356;
Fuel, 2024, 369, 131788; ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 13423). It is finding that our work first
proposed and confirmed that liquid metals can solve the problem of severe sintering of
single atoms under extremely high-temperature conditions, which was not reported before.
Therefore, the core innovation of work and the previously reported works are
essentially different. We don't think these articles conflict.

Reply to the referees
To Referee #4
First of all, thank you very much for your evaluation of our work. According to your suggestion,
we have supplemented a point-to-point reply with systematic experiments and discussions. We hope
that our revised manuscript is considered to be published in Nature Communications.
Overall remark: In the manuscript entitled “Liquid metal dispersed single-atom catalyst with
high-temperature stability” submitted to Nat. Commun., Zeng et al. report a Pt-based single-atom
catalyst dispersed in a Ga-based molten phase and supported on ZSM-5 for ethane dehydrogenation
to ethylene. The authors imply that this constitutes a new conceptual way of stabilizing SACs with
high activity and thermal stability, and they support their arguments by a combination of experimental
data and AIMD calculations.
Author reply: Thanks a lot for your evaluation that “this constitutes a new conceptual way of
stabilizing SACs with high activity and thermal stability, and they support their arguments by a
combination of experimental data and AIMD calculations.” Regarding the following detailed
questions that you put forward, we have supplemented systematic experiments and discussions,
including the core innovation of our work, the generalizability of our findings, reaction kinetic
analysis, the long-term stability, deactivation pathways, and structure-performance relationships. We
believe that the novelty, generalizability, and depth of our work have been greatly improved by your
insightful suggestion.
Comment 1: My main concern is that the central experimental claim about the unique role of Pt
is not convincingly supported by the data as described. The authors state in their rebuttal letter that,
upon “comparing the conversion and selectivity of pure ZSM-5, pure Ga, and Pt@Ga/ZSM-5,
it is obvious that both ZSM-5 and Ga have no impact on the activity.” This is difficult to
reconcile with the reported performance: Ga metal alone reaches approximately half the conversion of the Pt–Ga
single-atom system and even exhibits higher selectivity to ethylene. These numbers strongly suggest
that Ga is an active and selective catalyst on its own and that the incremental contribution of Pt to
the overall performance is limited. Rather than demonstrating a clear, dominant role of Pt single
atoms in a molten Ga host, the data point to a system in which Ga already performs well and Pt
provides a modest, enhancement in conversion at (perhaps) the cost of selectivity. The authors need
to acknowledge and analyze this more carefully; in its current form, the narrative that Ga and ZSM-
5 “have no impact on the activity” is not credible.
Author reply: Thank you very much for your constructive feedback on our revised manuscript.
Regarding your questions about the contribution of Ga, and Pt to the overall ethane dehydrogenation
(EDH) performance, we conducted supplementary experiments. The results indicate that Ga and
ZSM-5 do not provide additional catalytically active sites for EDH. Ga mainly serves as a dispersion
carrier, enabling high catalytic activity by dispersing metal Pt particles into single atoms. And the
ZSM-5 was used to enhance the gas mass transfer. The detailed analysis is listed below:
(1) Regarding whether Ga or ZSM-5 is an active and selective catalyst on its own, we
supplemented experiments with blank U-tubes. Due to the fluidity of liquid metal Ga, conventional
U-tubes cannot meet the requirements for EDH testing. In this work, we customized a home-made
U-tube equipped with a quartz sieve plate to support the catalyst as well as to enhance the mass
transfer (Fig. R1). Under identical catalytic conditions, the catalytic performance of the blank U-tube
and pure Ga (pure Ga@U-tube) is shown in Fig. R2. The ethane conversion and ethylene selectivity
of the U-tube are derived from the thermal cracking reaction of ethane. Comparison of catalytic
performance reveals that the ethane conversion of pure Ga, and the blank U-tube remains essentially
consistent, suggesting that Ga does not provide additional catalytically active sites. Regarding the
activity ZSM-5, the ZSM-5 (Si/Al = 45) used in our work is usually considered to exhibit negligible
activity for ethane dehydrogenation to ethylene, and substantial catalytic performance is typically
achieved through constructing tailored active sites via the surface immobilization of metal
nanoparticles (ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 9970) or the encapsulation of clusters or isolated metal sites
within its framework (Appl. Surf. Sci. 2021, 554, 149611; Chem 2023, 9, 637).
Fig. R1 | Schematic diagram of a quartz tube with a quartz sieve plate. The porous quartz sieve plate is
designed to prevent liquid metal leakage.
Fig. R2 | Comparison of catalytic performance of blank U-tube, and pure Ga. (a) Conversion of ethane.
(b) Selectivity of ethylene.
(2) Ga mainly acts as a dispersion support to enable the monodispersed state of Pt atoms,
which enhances the ethane conversion and ethylene selectivity. To further demonstrate the role of
Ga, we compared the catalytic performance of Pt particles@ZSM-5 (direct mixing of commercialized
Pt particles with ZSM-5 without utilizing Ga as dispersion) with that of Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5. Pt
particles@ZSM-5 exhibited ethane conversion at 9.5% and ethylene selectivity at 82.6% (Fig. R3).
In contrast, the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst, where Pt dissolves as single atoms within liquid Ga,
achieves a significantly higher ethane conversion (17.8%) while maintaining excellent ethylene
selectivity (98.3%). The breakthrough in performance stems from the introduction of liquid metal,
which directly alters the dispersed state of Pt atoms (Fig. 2e, f in the revised manuscript). By
dispersing Pt particles into single Pt atoms, the utilization of Pt atoms was maximized to achieve high
ethane conversion. Furthermore, the coordination environment of active metals significantly
influences the reaction selectivity. Usually, Pt particles with a non-uniform coordination environment
typically promote C−C cleavage and deep dehydrogenation side reactions (ACS Catal. 2020, 10,
12932). In contrast, Pt-based SACs with a uniform coordination environment exhibit excellent
selectivity for ethylene due to their superior activation of C−H bonds in alkanes, while simultaneously
limiting C−C bond cleavage to prevent dehydrogenation reactions. Therefore, the introduction of
liquid metal, which stabilizes Pt in a single-atom state with a highly uniform coordination
environment, allows the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst to reach an ethylene selectivity of 98.3%.
Taken together with the evidence that metallic Ga is catalytically inert (Fig. R2), we conclude that Ga
acts as a liquid dispersion to scatter and stabilize Pt atoms.

Conversion of ethane. b Selectivity of ethylene.

particular by Peter Wasserscheid and co-workers and others, who have explicitly discussed high-

Author reply: Thank you very much for your feedback on our revised manuscript. In terms of
the difference in our work and the reported SCALMS, especially the reference (doi:
10.1002/cphc.202400651), we have conducted a comprehensive literature search via SCOPUS. We
acknowledged that Prof. Peter and his colleagues, as well as others, have conducted important
research in this field. However, the core innovation of our work is different from that of the reported
works.
Our work focuses on the severe sintering limitation of SACs at high temperatures in
industrial catalysis. By leveraging the fluidity and metal affinity of liquid metal, we realized the
ultra-stable SACs at 650 oC for 100 hours. It is worth noting that the high temperature contributes
to the dispersion of single atoms in our work rather than the agglomeration sintering phenomenon in
reported works, which is owing to the selective breaking and formation of chemical bonds profiting
from the inherent metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal,
active metal atoms can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as a single-atom state at high
temperatures. This finding is of great significance for promoting the industrial application of SACs.
And we provided robust evidence through a combination of theoretical calculations and
experimental data (Fig. 2, Fig. 4 and Supplementary Movs. 1, 2 in the revised manuscript).
Additionally, immobilizing Ga–Pt on porous ZSM-5 is mainly to enhance the gas mass transfer
efficiency. The focus in this work is to utilize liquid metal to address the bottleneck of agglomeration
of SACs.
While the reference (doi:10.1002/cphc.202400651) focuses on the Ga–Ni system within
SCALMS for selective polymerization of ethylene. The active center of the catalyst is jointly
formed by isolated Ni single atoms and Ga–Ni intermetallic compounds (e.g., Ga Ni, Ga₇Ni₃),
5
which is different from the isolated single atoms as active centers in our work. However, at elevated
temperatures, the low-melting-point Ga₅Ni undergoes a phase transformation into the high-
melting-point Ga₇Ni₃ intermetallic compounds (Fig. R4a). Due to the insolubility Ga₇Ni₃, Ga₇Ni₃
cannot replenish Ni single atoms on the catalyst surface (Fig. R4b), leading to gradual depletion of
active sites and subsequent deterioration of catalyst stability (Fig. R4c). Therefore, the core
innovation, the stability of the catalyst, and structure-performance relationship of the reference
are totally different from our work.
Fig. R4 | Deactivation Mechanism of Ga–Ni SCALMS. a Snapshots of in situ SAED at 298 K, 553 K and
temperatures ranging from 473 to 623 K.
Furthermore, the synthetic approaches of our work and the reported SCALMS by Prof. Peter are
different. And the stability at high temperatures of our catalyst is outstanding among these
reported works.
1) A fundamental difference in the synthetic approaches. The approach of Prof. Peter
predominantly relies on galvanic replacement driven by differences in reduction potential (Nat. Chem.
2017, 9, 862) or impregnation-reduction (ChemCatChem, 2025, e202402096), whereby the salt of
the active metal reacts at the liquid Ga surface. However, galvanic replacement presents certain
limitations. One constraint is the uniformity of synthesis. The local electric field, ion concentration,
and the distribution of reactants will result in differences in size, composition, distribution, or
structure of the active sites formed through galvanic replacement reactions. Another limitation is
restricted universality. Electrodeposition requires a potential difference between the two metals,
meaning only metals with lower electrode potentials can replace those with higher potentials.
In contrast, our work employs the direct dissolution of metallic Pt into liquid Ga. By
leveraging the solvent properties of liquid metal and its strong affinity for Pt, we achieve stable Ga–
Pt interactions even at high temperatures, thereby efficiently forming highly uniform catalysts.
This highly uniform environment provides an efficient synthetic pathway for producing SACs with a
highly uniform coordination environment. Furthermore, Ga exhibits the favorable affinity and
relatively negative mixing enthalpy toward most metallic elements (Nature 2023, 619, 73), suggesting
the potential for universal synthesis of liquid metal dispersed SACs.
2) The superior thermal stability of the catalyst in our work. By comparing the operating
temperatures and time on stream of catalysts in our work versus Prof. Peter’s (Tab. R1), it is found
that the catalysts in our work reveal a distinct advantage in thermal stability. In the reported work of
Prof. Peter that catalysts were synthesized by the galvanic replacement method, active metals are
initially enriched at the surface or interface. Besides, high-temperature calcination is typically
required in this method to form the final SCALMS structure. At elevated temperatures, irreversible
transformations of the active sites lead to deactivation of the catalyst. Conversely, our catalyst
can maintain a stable single-atom state continuously without undergoing deactivation (evidenced by
XAFS in Figs. 4 e, f and theoretical calculation in Fig. 2). This exceptional thermal stability stems
from the stable interaction between Pt and Ga at high temperatures, which is a thermodynamically
driven process. This has been thoroughly evidenced at the atomic level from thermodynamic and
kinetic perspectives in Fig. 2 in our revised manuscript.
