In summary, through comparative analysis, we found that our work exhibits a fundamental
difference in core innovation, synthetic approach, and the stability of the active centers compared to
previously reported work. It is not merely an incremental advancement of prior research but
represents an entirely new concept. We present a new approach to achieve highly thermal-stable
SACs by dispersing metal Pt into single atoms by liquid metal Ga, which is driven by the stable Pt–
Ga interaction even at elevated temperatures. This is a thermodynamically driven process, and the
corresponding mechanism was thoroughly evidenced from both thermodynamic and kinetic
perspectives.
Changes: For highlighting the advantages of our work, the stability of the reported SACs and
ours has been summarized as Supplementary Tab. 1 in the revised manuscript.
Comment 3: In addition, the experimental scope is rather narrow for a paper targeting Nature
Communications. The study focuses on a single reaction (ethane to ethylene) under relatively limited
conditions, with a small set of catalyst formulations and without an in-depth kinetic analysis (e.g.
an estimate of turnover frequencies per Pt vs. Ga, reaction orders) or operando characterization that
would firmly establish the structure and environment of the proposed Pt single atoms under working
conditions. Long-term stability, deactivation pathways, and structure-performance relationships are
not explored to the depth one would expect for the broad readership of such a journal. The resulting
dataset is essentially a proof of concept confined to one reaction and one composition space, which
may be more appropriate for a specialized catalysis journal.
Author reply: Thank you very much for your constructive comments, which have significantly
helped us to enhance the depth and breadth of our work. In response to the concerns regarding the
scope of our experiments, we have supplemented the systematic supplementary studies and
discussions to analyze the applicability of the reaction system of our materials, reaction kinetic
analysis, the generalizability of our findings, and the long-term stability, deactivation pathways, and
structure-performance relationships. The detailed clarification is as follows:
(1) Regarding the catalysis reaction applicability of this catalyst, EDH was chosen as a proof
of concept, whose catalytic stability is highly sensitive to the dispersion state and coordination
environment of the active metals (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409784). Usually, when the
size of the active metals is increased, the coordination environment of each active atom is highly non-
uniform. This will typically promote C−C cleavage and deep dehydrogenation side reactions, which
severely hinder the stability of the catalyst (ACS Catal. 2020, 10, 12932). Therefore, EDH serves as
an exceptionally sensitive probe reaction for revealing the high-temperature stability of our
liquid-metal-supported SACs.
The core innovation of our work lies in addressing the problem of severe sintering of SACs
operated at high-temperature conditions in thermocatalysis by leveraging the fluidity and metal
affinity of liquid metal. Profiting from the superior metal affinity of Ga with Pt, Pt–Pt bonds are
broken at elevated temperatures, and subsequently the mobile Pt atoms are captured by Ga to form
the stable Pt–Ga interaction, accomplishing the highly efficient dispersion of Pt single atoms.
The fluidity of liquid metal and the stable Pt–Ga interaction ensure that the Pt atoms can remain
dynamically scattered throughout the whole liquid metal dispersion system. Additionally, liquid metal
dispersed single atoms can self-update onto the catalysis interface continuously, promoting catalytic
reactions at the interface. Hence, these liquid metal-dispersed SACs manifested remarkable thermal
durability and excellent ethylene selectivity for EDH.
Profiting from the favorable stability of the synthesized SACs, this approach is anticipated
to be extendable to other thermocatalysis reactions, such as CO₂ hydrogenation, reverse water-gas
shift reactions, selective hydrogenation, coupling reactions, alkene epoxidation, and Fenton-like
reactions, etc. These reactions occur under heating or even high-temperature conditions, imposing
higher demands on the thermal stability of catalysts. And multiple side reactions are prone to occur,
necessitating a highly uniform coordination environment around the catalytic active site to minimize
or suppress the occurrence of these side reactions. Our strategy holds promise for achieving high
stability and selectivity in these reactions. Accordingly, applying these catalysts to broader reaction
systems will be another major focus of our future work.
(2) In terms of the catalyst formulations, the concept of liquid metal-dispersed SACs can be
applied to synthesizing Rh-based SACs (Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM), and this catalyst also
demonstrates the improved EDH performance. In response to reviewer requests, we selected the
GaRh system to demonstrate the universality of this approach for synthesizing liquid metal-dispersed
SACs. XAFS analysis confirmed the formation of distinct Ga–Rh bonds (Fig. R5). Furthermore, the
synthesized Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM was employed in the EDH. The Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst
achieved an ethane conversion rate of 16.9% and an ethylene selectivity of 91.3% ( The atomic ratio
of Ga and Rh in this catalyst is 99.8 : 0.2). While the Rh particles/ZSM-5 exhibited only 13.2%
conversion and a mere 81.4% ethylene selectivity under the same amount of Rh (Fig. R6). Thus, the
synthesis method in our work exhibits certain applicability and can be extended to other catalyst
formulations.

Author reply: Thank you very much for your feedback on our revised manuscript. Our work
proposed a solution for agglomeration of SACs in industrial thermal catalytic processes. This finding
is substantiated through theoretical calculations and XAFS analysis before and after catalytic reaction.
It fundamentally differs from the innovations reported in previous SCALMS, SAC, and SAA studies.
Regarding the roles of Pt and Ga, we re-conducted tests following your suggestion and found Pt
to be the primary active site, while Ga does not directly contribute to the catalytic conversion.
However, Ga enables Pt particles to disperse into Pt single atoms, achieving breakthroughs in
selectivity and conversion. We have revised the data and descriptions in the paper accordingly.
Kinetic analysis further revealed that using liquid metal to disperse Pt from particles into single atoms
significantly reduces the activation energy for the EDH reaction.
To address limitations in the experimental scope, we extended the system from Pt to Rh and
confirmed the universality of the synthesis strategy via XAFS. Catalytic activity was also validated
through the EDH reaction, demonstrating superior selectivity and conversion rates compared to Rh
particles. We believe this approach has the potential to be extended to broader systems.

Overall remark: This manuscript reports a liquid metal catalytic system in which Pt dissolved
in liquid Ga exhibits exceptionally stable performance in ethane dehydrogenation. Although the
concept of using liquid metals in catalysis is not entirely new, the remarkable long-term stability
demonstrated here is still appealing. The theoretical analysis, especially the MD simulations,
on the thermodynamic stability of the single-atom Pt species is also insightful. In my view, this work
is suitable for publication in Nature Communications.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Single-atom catalysts (SACs) enable greener and more economically sustainable chemical production by significantly improving thermocatalysis efficiency and selectivity through maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environments. Unfortunately, SACs are fundamentally constrained by the stability owing to the severe aggregation of single atoms, especially under the high-temperature thermocatalysis operations, which compromises the overall catalytic performance. Here, we report a synthetic strategy to realize the highly thermal-stable SACs resistance to sintering at harsh conditions through harnessing the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. A stable liquid metal-active metal interaction is formed, profiting from the superior metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal, active metal atoms can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as the metallic single-atom state at high temperatures. This catalyst exhibits outstanding thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation, sustaining stable operation for over 100 h at 650 oC with an impressive ethylene selectivity of 98%. The strategy of constructing stable metal-metal interactions by utilizing the inherent metal affinity and dynamic fluidity of liquid metal will pave a practical way for the design of highly thermal-stable SACs.

---

## Introduction

Industrial thermocatalysis holds great promise for improving the efficiency and sustainability of thermochemical processes and producing value-added chemicals in the modern chemical industry1–3. Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have garnered extensive attention for the development of highly efficient, sustainable, cost-effective catalysts in thermocatalysis fields due to their maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environment4–8.

However, constructing highly thermally durable SACs is a significant challenge in industrial applications. This is owing to the inherently ultra-high surface energy of single atoms, and the high temperature (> 300 oC) provides enough energy to overcome the diffusion barrier of single atoms, leading to the migration of single atoms and severe agglomeration9. In the current paradigm, it is prevalent to stabilize SACs by modulating supports (such as carbon-based supports10, metal oxides characterized by defection11–14, and so on) that tune interactions between metal atoms and supports. However, the presence of a strong bonding interaction between the supports and the single atoms may result in the compromise of the unique coordination structure of the single atoms, thereby diminishing the catalytic activity and even deactivation15,16. In terms of the strategy of using porous supports to spatially confine single atoms (such as molecular sieves and metal-organic frameworks)17,18, surmounting the substantial surface energy of the single atoms is still difficult, which will lead to inevitable aggregation of single atoms at elevated temperatures19,20. Hence, designing an optimal support that balances metal-support interaction for realizing highly efficient thermal-stable SACs remains an obstacle.

Inspired by the rule of thumb “like dissolves like”, it is promising to take advantage of unique metal-metal interaction to efficiently disperse active metals to acquire stable single atoms with inherently high metal activity by using the liquid metal as the dispersion21–23. Herein, we achieve the highly efficient dispersion of single atoms with unprecedented thermal stability by utilizing the inherent fluidity and metal affinity of liquid metal. As a demonstration, gallium (Ga), capable of an ideal liquid environment, was employed to spontaneously disperse active metal platinum (Pt). Exceptionally thermal-stable Pt single atoms dispersed by Ga that survived at 650 oC were realized. In this system, profiting from the superior metal affinity of Ga with Pt, Pt–Pt bonds are broken at elevated temperatures, and subsequently the mobile Pt atoms are captured by Ga to form the stable Pt–Ga interaction, accomplishing the highly efficient dispersion of Pt single atoms. The fluidity of liquid metal and the stable Pt–Ga interaction ensure that the Pt atoms can remain dynamically scattered throughout the whole liquid metal dispersion system. Additionally, liquid metal dispersed single atoms can self-update onto the catalysis interface continuously, promoting catalytic reactions at the interface. Hence, these liquid metal dispersed SACs manifested remarkable thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation (EDH), sustaining stable operation for over 100 hours at 650 oC with ethylene selectivity of 98%. Furthermore, the elemental composition of the system was extended to other noble metals, demonstrating the universality of the synthetic strategy. This elucidates the promising potential in realizing highly thermal-stable SACs.

---

## Results

The design of thermal-stable liquid metal dispersed SACs

With increasing temperature, the diffusivity of single atoms is accelerated, thereby enhancing their migration and subsequent aggregation into larger clusters or particles due to thermodynamics favoring lower total surface energy states9,24. In essence, the competition of aggregation reflected the competitive bonding between single atom/single atom and single atom/support. Establishing highly efficient as well as stable metal-support interaction is crucial for blocking the aggregation and sintering of single atoms at high temperatures. In this work, we make the realization of thermal-stable SACs by utilizing liquid metal to disperse and stabilize active metals (Fig. 1a). The abundance of metallic bonds in the liquid metal makes it an ideal medium for effectively dispersing active metals with similar metallic bonds, and the active metals can keep the metallic state. At elevated temperatures, enough energy is provided to break metallic bonds in the active metals. Furthermore, the fluidity of liquid metals drives the dispersion of active atoms in liquid metals at elevated temperatures. These dynamically migrating single atoms can be subsequently combined with liquid metal, profiting from its good metallic affinity and forming a stable interaction between these two kinds of atoms. In light of this, equipped with the naturally metallic affinity and fluidity of liquid metal, the highly thermal-stable SACs can be realized.

The liquid metal dispersed SACs are synthesized by dissolving Pt nanoparticles into liquid Ga at elevated temperatures. The mechanism illustrating the formation process of the liquid metal dispersed SACs is shown in Fig. 1a. Firstly, the Pt particles were sprinkled evenly over the liquid metal. As the temperature gradually increases, the solubility of the active metal in the dispersion is further increased, and the active metal can efficiently disperse in the liquid metal within its limited solubility. The Pt−Pt bonds in the original Pt metal nanoparticles are broken and tend to bind tightly to Ga atoms and form a thermodynamically stable configuration with Ga atoms, benefiting from the good affinity between Ga and Pt. The stable Pt−Ga interaction curtails the sintering of Pt single atoms. Moreover, according to the Arrhenius equation25, the thermal motion of atoms would be intensified by high temperature, promoting the rapid diffusion between Pt and Ga atoms and the continuous renewal of Pt single atoms exposed on the catalytic surface (Fig. 1b). In contrast, when single atoms are anchored to solid supports, their co-migration with the supports becomes kinetically constrained. Once the metal-support interactions become insufficient to compensate for the inherently high surface energy of single atoms, these atoms tend to detach from the solid supports and aggregate. This process is exothermic, where minimization of total surface energy governs particle growth26. Meanwhile, some single atoms may embed into the lattice of supports, becoming buried when the interaction between the support and metal atoms is too strong. These lead to the loss of active sites, reducing the stability of SACs and consequently affecting their activity and selectivity (Fig. 1c).

Thermal stability of active metal atoms mono-dispersed in liquid Ga

Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were employed to elucidate the atomic-scale dispersed state of active metal in liquid metal (computational details are provided in the supplementary information). Using Pt as a model of Pt cluster, we investigated the structural evolution of both clustered and dispersed Pt in liquid Ga during 10 ps simulations at 923 K (Figs. 2a, b and Supplementary Movs. 1, 2). The calculated total energy versus time curves for the Ga Pt system containing clustered Pt and dispersed Pt (Fig. 2c) reveal that the dispersed Pt generally exhibits lower total energy compared to the aggregated Pt clusters within the simulated 10 ps. The results indicate that the remarkable atomic diffusion of liquid Ga metal at high temperature promotes the migration of heterogeneous active metal atoms, thereby stabilizing their dispersed atomic state in liquid Ga.

The relatively high Pt concentration in the Ga Pt system leads to intermittent formation of Pt dimer, as evidenced by the time-dependent curve of the shortest Pt–Pt distance (Supplementary Fig. 1). To further elucidate the actual existence state of Pt atoms in liquid Ga, we performed AIMD simulations of the Ga Pt system (a Pt dimer embedded in Ga ) at 923 K. The 10 ps NVT ensemble simulations (Fig. 2d) display that the Pt–Pt interatomic distance progressively increases from 4.18 Å to 11.63 Å, significantly exceeding the Pt–Pt bond length of 2.65 ~ 2.79 Å28. This unequivocally confirms that Pt atoms preferentially exist as monatomic species in the liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Movs. 3, 4). Further statistical analysis of the coordination environment of Pt atoms in the Ga Pt system shows that the dominant coordination numbers for individual Pt atoms are 8 or 9 (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4), implying that mono-dispersed Pt atoms migrate within liquid Ga in the form of clusters such as Ga Pt or Ga Pt (Supplementary Fig. 5).

To fundamentally understand the thermodynamic preference for Pt mono-dispersion in liquid Ga, we systematically calculated the bond energy difference ∆E (∆𝐸 = 𝐸 + 𝐸̅ −2𝐸 ) only for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figs. 6 ~ 11). Here, 𝐸̅ represents the average Ga–Ga bond energy in the Ga molecular clusters, 𝐸 denotes the Pt–Pt bond energy in the (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, and 𝐸 refers to the Ga–Pt bond energy in the Ga Pt molecular clusters. The results indicate that the ∆E values for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, evaluated using different computational methods (B3LYP, MN15L, and M06L), are all greater than zero. This demonstrates that in these molecular systems, the Ga atoms involved in bond-breaking readily disrupt the Pt–Pt bonds, leading to the formation of stable Pt–Ga–Pt bridging units, thereby promoting the single-atom dispersion of Pt in liquid Ga. Meanwhile, we calculated the formation energies of Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga molecules, which were determined to be 101.1, 46.2, and 57.9 kcal mol–1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12 and Fig. 2f). Additionally, we roughly estimated the energy barriers of Ga atom insertion into the Pt–Pt bond to be 58.2, 13.4, and 40.2 kcal mol–1 by performing rigid scans of the Pt–Ga–Pt angle (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Fig. 2f). These results clearly demonstrate that, both thermodynamically and kinetically, Ga atoms in liquid Ga at 923 K can readily disrupt Pt–Pt bonds, thereby promoting the mono-dispersion of Pt atoms.

To more intuitively demonstrate the mono-dispersion state of Pt atoms in Ga, we constructed Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures with Pt contents of 2 at% and 0.2 at%, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 14). Meanwhile, based on a training dataset containing 17347 structures and a test dataset of 1926 structures, we trained a Ga–Pt neuroevolution potential model (Supplementary Fig. 15). The consistency between the calculated and experimental solubility validates the effectiveness of the constructed machine learning force field in evaluating the dissolution of Pt in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 16). Subsequently, we performed 20 ns NVT molecular dynamics simulations at 923 K on the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures using the trained Ga–Pt machine-learning potential. The simulation results clearly indicate that the Pt cluster rapidly disperse in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, we analyzed the proportions of mono-dispersed and dimerized Pt states in all structures over the last 10 ns (Fig. 2g). In the Ga Pt structure, the proportion of mono-dispersed Pt was 98.2%, while in the Ga Pt structure, it reached 99.9%. The results clearly demonstrate that in structures with Pt content of 2 at% or below, Pt atoms can be considered fully mono-dispersed at 923 K. Moreover, the calculated average numbers of surface atoms in the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures are 5.4 and 3.0, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 18 and Supplementary Fig. 19), and the temporal evolution of the vertical migration of individual Pt atoms and their probability distribution demonstrate a preferential tendency to migrate toward the surface (Supplementary Fig. 20). These indicate that a certain proportion of mono-dispersed Pt atoms can continuously exist on the liquid surface and participate in relevant catalytic reactions. Overall, the stable Ga Pt and similar clusters that are formed profited from the favorable affinity between Ga and Pt inhibit the aggregation and sintering of Pt during thermal motion, laying the foundation for synthesizing the highly thermal-stable SACs.

Characterization of liquid catalyst

To further validate that liquid metal can act as the dispersion for single atoms, we synthesized the Ga-dispersed Pt SACs (Pt SACs@Ga). The detailed structure of the catalyst was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The Pt species in the liquid metal exists in a mono-disperse distribution without the obvious occurrence of aggregated Pt (Fig. 3a). The bright-field image of Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst maintains an almost invariant brightness across the whole particle and the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) data shows no diffraction spots of Pt in the amorphous ring, revealing the lack of long-range order structure in the Ga–Pt catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Fig. 3b). Furthermore, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum was employed to reveal the chemical composition and electronic structure of the liquid metal dispersed SACs. Before the execution of XPS measurements, the sample underwent etching with argon ions to eliminate the natural oxide layer and surface contaminants. Ga 2p peaks appear at 1116.73 eV and 1116.59 eV (Fig. 3c), which are consistent with the reported binding energies of metallic Ga (Ga0 2p =1116.70 eV). Meanwhile, due to the higher electronegativity of Pt (2.28) than that of Ga (1.81)29, the Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga system served as the electron acceptor, and the Pt 4f and 4f peaks in Pt SACs@Ga exhibit a positive shift (1.0 eV) than those in pure Pt metal (Fig. 3d). It is a consensus that metallic Pt0 species occupy a preeminent role as the active sites for many catalytic processes30–32. This guarantees a proficient and robust distribution of single atoms while preserving their catalytic activity. Furthermore, the absence of the obvious aggregation of Pt atoms in the Pt SACs@Ga is further identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) tests, where no signal of Pt (PDF#04-0802) is observed (Supplementary Fig. 22). To mitigate the potential inaccuracies arising from the insensitivity of XRD to small Pt clusters, the pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was conducted to delve into the interatomic structure of the Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 23). The absence of Pt–Pt bonds indicates that Pt is distributed nearly at the atomic level within the liquid Ga without the formation of Pt clusters. These observations suggest that liquid metal can achieve the efficient uniform dispersion of highly active single atoms at elevated temperatures.

To further verify the exact dispersion state of Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga catalyst, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were conducted. The X-ray absorption edge near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum shows that the intensity of the white line at the L edge of Pt lies between that of the Pt foil and that of PtO . Correspondingly, the k -weighted R-space Fourier transformed spectra of the extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectra (EXAFS) show the prominent peak at 2.14 Å for Pt SACs@Ga distinguished from that of the Pt–O (1.62 Å) bonds for PtO and the Pt–Pt bonds (2.24 Å) for Pt foil (Fig. 3f). All these results intuitively indicate that the Pt exists in the single-atom state in liquid metal.

EDH performance of liquid metal dispersed SACs

Based on the computational results, the liquid metal dispersed SACSs theoretically feature excellent thermal stability at high temperatures. It is necessary to conduct specific high-temperature tests for verification. Pt-based catalysts are used for the dehydrogenation of alkanes due to their high efficiency in activating the C−H bonds of alkanes and low propensity in breaking C−C bonds33,34. And Pt−Sn/Al O (Oleflex process) is the primary industrial technology operated for direct propane dehydrogenation35. While it suffers from severe sintering and coke, which results in rapid deactivation and restricts the selectivity36. Therefore, as a proof of concept, the thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs was validated by EDH. As shown in Fig. 4a, when exposed to ethane, Pt single atoms exposed on the surface capture ethane molecules and synergistically activate C–H bonds, leading to selective EDH to ethylene. Meanwhile, the fluidic characteristic of liquid metal dispersed SACs at operating conditions enables continuous replenishment of catalytically active Pt atoms onto the surface. The stable interaction between Pt−Ga effectively blocks the aggregation of Pt atoms during the constant migration. Benefiting from the advantages mentioned above, these adaptive surface active sites maintain long-term activity and thermal stability.

To circumvent the issue of inadequate interaction between the liquid metal dispersed SACs and the reaction gas, the porous support is utilized to amplify the gas mass transfer rate. So, we coupled liquid metal dispersed SACs with porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) by the physical approach of ultrasonication to increase the contact surface area between the liquid metal support SACs and gas reactants. As demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 24, EDS mappings revealed a well-distribution of Ga, Si, and Al, indicating the liquid metal is uniformly loaded in the ZSM-5 zeolite framework. Upon heating, Pt will be spontaneously dispersed in Ga homogeneously, achieving the preparation of a zeolite-dispersed liquid metal supported SACs (Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5). Further, we performed in situ XRD to explore the dispersing process of Pt (Supplementary Fig. 25). The diffraction peak observed at 43 ~ 47o originates from the carbon in situ reactor (Supplementary Fig. 26). Initially, the characteristic peaks of Pt can be apparently observed, which are located at 39.76o and 46.24o. With the temperature increasing, the characteristic peaks of Pt were gradually weakened and disappeared subsequently, proving the dispersion of Pt particles.

The catalytic performance was evaluated in non-oxidative EDH at 923 K in a fixed-bed quartz U-tube reactor under atmospheric pressure with a feed gas of 12.5 vol% C H in Ar. The Pt particles/ZSM-5 catalyst, which is synthesized by direct mixing commercial Pt particles with ZSM-5, exhibits ethane conversion at 9.5% and ethylene selectivity at 82.6% (Figs. 4b, c). Interestingly, the liquid metal dispersed SACs are highly active with ethane conversion at 17.8% and ethylene selectivity at 98.3%. This is because the introduction of liquid metal alters the state of Pt. By dispersing Pt particles into single Pt atoms, the utilization of Pt atoms is maximized to achieve high conversion rates. Furthermore, since the size of Pt particle significantly influences catalytic performance, larger Pt nanoparticles typically promote C−C cleavage and deep dehydrogenation side reactions37. In contrast, Pt-based catalysts dispersed at the atomic scale exhibit excellent selectivity for ethylene due to their superior activation of C−H bonds in alkanes, while simultaneously limiting C−C bond cleavage to prevent dehydrogenation reactions. Therefore, when liquid metal is introduced, Pt exists in a single-atom state, enabling the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst to achieve high selectivity. To verify the universality of the strategy that liquid metals can disperse metals into single atoms, we extended the synthesis approach to other systems and successfully synthesized liquid metal dispersed Rh SACs (Supplementary Fig. 27). Moreover, Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 exhibits significantly improved catalytic performance compared to Rh particles/ZSM-5 in EDH (Supplementary Fig. 28).

To gain a deeper understanding of the effects of liquid metal dispersed SACs and nano catalysts on the dehydrogenation reaction of ethane, we conducted kinetic studies on both types of catalysts. We measured the ethane conversion in a temperature range of 883 ~ 933 K and fitted the data according to the Arrhenius equation to calculate the apparent activation energy for EDH. The apparent activation energies for Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 and Pt particles/ZSM-5 are 102.44 kJ mol−1 and 137.18 kJ mol−1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 29). The significantly reduced activation energy indicates a decreased energy barrier that needs to be overcome for the reaction to proceed. And the single Pt atom dispersed in the liquid Ga can more effectively weaken the C–H bond of ethane than Pt particles. Therefore, the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibits superior catalytic performance.

The performance of the liquid metal dispersed SACs in the durability test is presented in Fig. 4d. It exhibits sustainable conversion and selectivity in the continuous reaction for 100 h, where the constant ethane conversion of ~18% is obtained without attenuation. And liquid metal dispersed SACs exhibit a steady ethene productivity of around 14.3 g g −1 h−1 during the 100 h Pt EDH test. The catalyst displays no deactivation trend during the testing period, indicating a reasonable expectation of more durable stability. Notably, the XANES spectrum and R-space of liquid metal dispersed SACs after 100 h EDH at Pt L -edge are similar to those of pristine liquid SACs (Figs. 4e, f and Figs. 3e, f), demonstrating exceptional structural integrity under prolonged thermal catalysis. The catalytic performance and structural characterization together confirmed the superior thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs in extremely high temperatures, which remarkably outperforms the traditional solid support loaded SACs. To further substantiate the thermal stability performance of our work, comparing the catalytic reaction temperatures and time on stream of Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 with reported SACs (Supplementary Tab. 1), where the results remain outstanding. The excellent stability, selectivity, and conversion indicate the potential of liquid metal dispersed SACs for reactions limited in harsh conditions.

---

## Methods

Chemicals and materials

Gallium (Ga, 99.999%) was purchased from Shanghai Minor Metals Co. Ltd., platinum (Pt, 99.9%) and molecular sieve (ZSM-5 zeolites, Si/Al = 45) were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Inc. Rhodium (Rh, 99.95%) powder was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. High-purity ethane (99.99%) was purchased from Wuhan Xiangyun Gas Technology Co., Ltd. and was purified using 4A zeolite before reaction.

Catalyst synthesis

Synthesis of liquid metal dispersed SACs

The liquid metal dispersed SACs were synthesized by dissolving Pt or Rh nanoparticles into molten Ga in a tube furnace in a H /Ar mixture gas at 650 oC, with a heating rate of 5 oC min–1.

Synthesis of the catalyst for EDH

In order to increase the mass transfer of the ethane, the liquid metal is coupled with the ZSM-5 (Ga/ZSM-5) by sonication as follows. The liquid Ga and ZSM-5 zeolites were transferred to ethylene glycol, and the solution was sonicated by a probe-type sonicator for 2 h (5 s on and 3 s off) at a power of 290 W. After sonication, the resultant precipitations were washed with ethanol and water 3 times. And then the resultant was flash frozen in liquid nitrogen for five minutes and freeze-dried at −40 oC, under a pressure less than 200 mTorr, for 24 h using the FreeZone 4.5 Liter Benchtop Freeze Dry System. The Pt particles were mixed with Ga/ZSM-5 (or pure ZSM-5) and heated from room temperature to 650 oC at a rate of 10 oC min–1 in the reactor under a H /Ar mixed gas atmosphere. The mixture was then held at 650 oC for 30 minutes to complete the synthesis of the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst (or Pt particles/ZSM-5). The Pt : Ga atomic ratio of the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst prepared for catalytic testing was maintained at 0.2 : 99.8. After purging the H from the U-tube, the catalyst was ready for catalytic testing. Similarly, replace the Pt particles with Rh particles and undergo the same treatment to obtain Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 (or Rh particles/ZSM-5), and the Rh : Ga atomic ratio of the Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst used for catalytic testing is also maintained at 0.2 : 99.8.

Catalyst characterizations

The morphology of the liquid metal dispersed SACs was characterized by an F200 transmission electron microscope (TEM) (JEOL, Japan) operated at 200 kV. X-ray diffraction (XRD) data was employed by PANalytical X’Pert-Pro diffractometer, with a Cu K𝛼 radiation (𝜆 = 0.15406 nm), in the 2θ scan mode ranging from 10o to 80o at a scan speed of 8o min−1. In situ XRD was collected with the Rigaku Ultima Ⅳ instrument using Cu Kα (λ = 1.5406 Å) radiation at 40 kV and 40 mA, and the operating voltage and current were 40 kV and 40 mA, respectively. The catalysts were scanned at a rate of 8o min−1 in the 2θ range of 35o ~ 60o. Pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was performed at room temperature in an air atmosphere by SmartLab, with a Ag K𝛼 radiation (𝜆 = 0.056088 nm). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were taken on a high-resolution Thermo Fisher Scientific ESCALAB Xi+ spectrometer using Al K𝛼 radiation under vacuum. Pt L and Rh K edge XAFS spectra were collected at the BL11B beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). During the measurement, the synchrotron radiation ring was operated at 3.5 GeV, and the electron current was 200 mA in the top-up mode. The samples were sealed in Kapton film. For the measurement of Pt L edge, the white light was monochromatized by a Si (111) double-crystal monochromator. And the white light was monochromatized by a Si (311) double-crystal monochromator when the Rh K edge was measured. The corresponding metal foils were used as a reference sample to calibrate and measure in the transmission mode. All XAFS spectra were processed using the IFEFFIT package. The elemental composition of the samples before and after the reaction was determined by inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES).

Catalytic performance and kinetic behavior measurements

EDH tests were performed under atmospheric pressure in a fixed-bed quartz U-tube reactor. Catalysts were weighed and loaded into 10 mm outside diameter, 8 mm interior diameter U-tube reactor. 5 sccm of argon and 15 sccm of hydrogen were flowed at 650 oC for 10 minutes to reduce any metal oxides. And then the reactor was purged with 20 sccm argon for 5 min to prevent hydrogen residue. The EDH reaction was conducted in a C H /Ar mixture gas (Vol C H /Vol Ar = 1:7) with a flow rate of 20 mL min−1. The outlet gas products were observed by an online mass spectrometer (Pro-tech, PM-QMS, China ). The conversion of ethane and selectivity to all carbonaceous products (including coke) were calculated as follows:

Ethane conversion = (molar flow rate of carbon (C) in products / molar flow rate of total C in effluent (C H +products)) * 100% (1)

Product selectivity = (molar flow rate of C in product i / molar flow rate of C in all products) * 100% (2)

The kinetic behavior of the catalyst for EDH needs to minimize transport limitations. Therefore, the conversion was limited to 5 ~ 15% while ethylene selectivity remained above 90% by systematically varying the catalyst amount. By analyzing the temperature and pressure dependence of these rates, we extracted the activation energy and reaction order for the reaction.

Theoretical calculations

Quantum chemistry calculations and Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations

To investigate the atomic-level dispersion of active metals in the liquid Ga, we initially constructed a Ga Pt cubic cell model using LAMMPS-17Apr2024 software. The initial cell parameter was set to 13 Å, with Pt as a cluster molecule and the remaining 90 Ga atoms randomly distributed. Subsequently, ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP.5.4.4) to the potential energy curves for both clustered and dispersed states of Pt in the Ga Pt structural model at 923 K. For the dispersed state, the damping coefficients for Ga and Pt were set to 10 and 5, respectively, while for the clustered state, they were set to 10 and 1000. All calculations were conducted using the GGA-PBEsol functional38 and employed the Langevin thermostat and ParrinIello-Rahman method39,40 for the isothermal-isobaric (nP T) ensemble. The cutoff energy was set to 400 eV with an energy convergence tolerance of 10–6 eV, and the simulation time was 10 ps. Due to the relatively high Pt content in the Ga Pt system, occasional Pt units were observed in the simulation results. Therefore, we further performed similar ab initio molecular dynamics simulations for the Ga Pt system, and an extra 10 ps NVT MD simulation was carried out starting from the last snapshot of the NPT simulation. Additionally, the crystalNN statistical method41 was used to evaluate the Pt–Pt bonding in liquid Ga. To gain further insight into the dispersion of Pt atoms in liquid Ga, we employed the B3LYP/LANL2DZ, MN15L/LANL2DZ42 and M06L/LANL2DZ methods to calculate the bond energy difference ∆E . The specific calculation method of ∆E for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters is based on Equation (3):

∆𝐸 = 𝐸 + 𝐸̅ −2𝐸 (3)

Here, 𝐸̅ represents the average Ga–Ga bond energy in the Ga molecular clusters, 𝐸 denotes the Pt–Pt bond energy in the (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, and 𝐸 refers to the Ga–Pt bond energy in the Ga Pt molecular clusters. All bond energy calculations were corrected for basis set superposition error (BSSE). Furthermore, we constructed cluster structures such as Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga, optimizing all cluster molecules using the B3LYP/LANL2DZ method. Additionally, we performed rigid scans of the PtGaPt angle in the Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga cluster systems to roughly estimate the energy barrier associated with the incorporation of Ga atoms into the Pt–Pt bond.

Ga–Pt machine learning force field training and molecular dynamics simulations

We constructed a dataset for the Ga–Pt binary system, comprising 17347 training structures and 1926 test structures. These structures cover bulk and surface structures of α-Ga, β-Ga, γ-Ga, Pt, Ga Pt, Ga Pt, Ga Pt , Ga Pt and Ga Pt , Ga–Pt bulk structures with varying compositions (Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , Ga Pt , and Ga Pt ). Nanoparticle systems such as Pt , Pt , Pt , and Pt were also considered. The dataset was initially generated using isothermal–isobaric (NPT) Ab initio molecular dynamics (MD) simulations under ambient pressure (0.0001 GPa) and temperatures ranging from 0 to 9000 K. A machine learning potential was trained using data from AIMD simulations.

Density functional theory calculations

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The calculations employed a plane-wave basis set with the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method and standard pseudo-potentials for Ga and Pt. The GGA-PBE sol density functional was selected, along with D3 dispersion interaction corrections. All calculations were conducted in high-precision mode (PREC = Accurate), with a plane-wave cutoff energy set to 400 eV and without symmetry constraints (ISYM = 0). To ensure accuracy, the electronic self-consistent loop converged to a tolerance of 10–6 eV (EDIFF = 1.0E–6). The Methfessel-Paxton first-order smearing method (ISMEAR = 1) was applied. The conjugate gradient algorithm was used for electronic minimization, and the maximum number of steps for electronic self-consistent (SCF) cycles was set to 999. A k-point mesh was automatically generated based on the reciprocal lattice vectors of the unit cell, with a k-point spacing of approximately 0.040 Å–1 in each direction. Only single-point calculations were performed, as the DFT computations were primarily used to generate labels for training data.

Machine learning force field training

The training of the force field is performed using the efficient Neural Evolutionary Potential (NEP) method and the GPUMD code. The training dataset is sourced from the previously completed PBE -D3 calculations. The cutoff radii for the radial and angular descriptors are set to 8 Å and 6 Å, respectively. The weights for energy, force, and virial stress are 1.0, 1.0, and 0.1, respectively. The number of neurons in the hidden layer of the neural network (NN) is 50. The NEP potential function underwent 200,000 optimization iterations over the entire training set. The final results include the root mean square errors (RMSE) of energy and atomic forces.

### Reviewer 1

The work by Ziyue Zeng's and coworkers deals with a very relevant topic in the field of catalysis. The paper is well written and contains relevant information. However, the paper is not suitable for Nature Communications and needs to be fundamentally revised in order to be suitable for a more specialised journal in the future. The reason is simple: the main claims of the article, namely that a single Pt atom can be stabilised in liquid gallium to perform high-temperature dehydrogenation catalysis in the form of supported liquid metal catalysis, are by no means new, but have already been published (with slightly different terminology) in more than 50 articles (this reviewer has verified this today using SCOPUS), including high-ranking publications in Nature Chemistry, such as the work by Rahim et al. in Nature Chemistry, Volume 14, 935-941 from 2022. (DOI: 10.1038/s41557-022-00965-6).
Even the idea to immobilize liquid Ga-Pt alloy droplets on porous supports for alkane dehydrogenation reactions is far from new. Under the name ‘Supported Catalytically Active Liquid Metal Solutions (SCALMS)’ (Nature Chemistry, 2017, 9(9), 862-867, DOI: 10.1038/nchem.2822, and paper citing this work) more than 30 paper have been published describing exactly this concept, 11 of these deal with Ga-Pt systems including preparation by ultrasonication and theoretical calculations to prove the isolated nature of Pt in Ga. Seven of these papers deal with propane dehydrogenation which is a very similar reaction to ethane hydrogenation.
In this light, this reviewer finds it striking that none of these earlier works were cited by Ziyue Zeng and coworkers. This is strange – and even if one takes into account the slightly different terminology used in the various articles – a proper and rigorous approach could have led to the conclusion that the work described in the current submission lacks the required novelty for a publication in Nature Communications.
In conclusion, this reviewer recommends studying the existing literature much more carefully and then publishing some of the interesting detailed information in the submitted manuscript in a much more specialised journal.

### Reviewer 2

In the manuscript, the authors described a strategy to realize the highly thermal-stable single-atom catalysts (SACs) resistance to sintering through harnessing the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. This work provides a novel approach for addressing the thermal instability of SACs under high-temperature conditions, which is regarded as the most critical and persistent challenge in single-atom catalysis. The proposed liquid metal-dispersed SACs exhibited outstanding thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation, sustaining stable operation for over 100 h at 650 oC with an impressive ethylene selectivity of 98%. Hence, I would like to recommend the publication in Nature Communications. The following are several minor details for the authors to consider:

## Paper

## Abstract

Single-atom catalysts (SACs) enable greener and more economically sustainable chemical production by significantly improving thermocatalysis efficiency and selectivity through maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environments. Unfortunately, SACs are fundamentally constrained by the stability owing to the severe aggregation of single atoms, especially under the high-temperature thermocatalysis operations, which compromises the overall catalytic performance. Here, we report a synthetic strategy to realize the highly thermal-stable SACs resistance to sintering at harsh conditions through harnessing the inherent metal affinity and fluidity of liquid metal. A stable liquid metal-active metal interaction is formed, profiting from the superior metal affinity of liquid metal. Combined with the fluidity of liquid metal, active metal atoms can move but remain confined to the liquid metal as the metallic single-atom state at high temperatures. This catalyst exhibits outstanding thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation, sustaining stable operation for over 100 h at 650 oC with an impressive ethylene selectivity of 98%. The strategy of constructing stable metal-metal interactions by utilizing the inherent metal affinity and dynamic fluidity of liquid metal will pave a practical way for the design of highly thermal-stable SACs.

---

## Introduction

Industrial thermocatalysis holds great promise for improving the efficiency and sustainability of thermochemical processes and producing value-added chemicals in the modern chemical industry1–3. Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have garnered extensive attention for the development of highly efficient, sustainable, cost-effective catalysts in thermocatalysis fields due to their maximized atom utilization and highly homogeneous metal coordination environment4–8.

However, constructing highly thermally durable SACs is a significant challenge in industrial applications. This is owing to the inherently ultra-high surface energy of single atoms, and the high temperature (> 300 oC) provides enough energy to overcome the diffusion barrier of single atoms, leading to the migration of single atoms and severe agglomeration9. In the current paradigm, it is prevalent to stabilize SACs by modulating supports (such as carbon-based supports10, metal oxides characterized by defection11–14, and so on) that tune interactions between metal atoms and supports. However, the presence of a strong bonding interaction between the supports and the single atoms may result in the compromise of the unique coordination structure of the single atoms, thereby diminishing the catalytic activity and even deactivation15,16. In terms of the strategy of using porous supports to spatially confine single atoms (such as molecular sieves and metal-organic frameworks)17,18, surmounting the substantial surface energy of the single atoms is still difficult, which will lead to inevitable aggregation of single atoms at elevated temperatures19,20. Hence, designing an optimal support that balances metal-support interaction for realizing highly efficient thermal-stable SACs remains an obstacle.

Inspired by the rule of thumb “like dissolves like”, it is promising to take advantage of unique metal-metal interaction to efficiently disperse active metals to acquire stable single atoms with inherently high metal activity by using the liquid metal as the dispersion21–23. Herein, we achieve the highly efficient dispersion of single atoms with unprecedented thermal stability by utilizing the inherent fluidity and metal affinity of liquid metal. As a demonstration, gallium (Ga), capable of an ideal liquid environment, was employed to spontaneously disperse active metal platinum (Pt). Exceptionally thermal-stable Pt single atoms dispersed by Ga that survived at 650 oC were realized. In this system, profiting from the superior metal affinity of Ga with Pt, Pt–Pt bonds are broken at elevated temperatures, and subsequently the mobile Pt atoms are captured by Ga to form the stable Pt–Ga interaction, accomplishing the highly efficient dispersion of Pt single atoms. The fluidity of liquid metal and the stable Pt–Ga interaction ensure that the Pt atoms can remain dynamically scattered throughout the whole liquid metal dispersion system. Additionally, liquid metal dispersed single atoms can self-update onto the catalysis interface continuously, promoting catalytic reactions at the interface. Hence, these liquid metal dispersed SACs manifested remarkable thermal durability for ethane dehydrogenation (EDH), sustaining stable operation for over 100 hours at 650 oC with ethylene selectivity of 98%. Furthermore, the elemental composition of the system was extended to other noble metals, demonstrating the universality of the synthetic strategy. This elucidates the promising potential in realizing highly thermal-stable SACs.

---

## Results

The design of thermal-stable liquid metal dispersed SACs

With increasing temperature, the diffusivity of single atoms is accelerated, thereby enhancing their migration and subsequent aggregation into larger clusters or particles due to thermodynamics favoring lower total surface energy states9,24. In essence, the competition of aggregation reflected the competitive bonding between single atom/single atom and single atom/support. Establishing highly efficient as well as stable metal-support interaction is crucial for blocking the aggregation and sintering of single atoms at high temperatures. In this work, we make the realization of thermal-stable SACs by utilizing liquid metal to disperse and stabilize active metals (Fig. 1a). The abundance of metallic bonds in the liquid metal makes it an ideal medium for effectively dispersing active metals with similar metallic bonds, and the active metals can keep the metallic state. At elevated temperatures, enough energy is provided to break metallic bonds in the active metals. Furthermore, the fluidity of liquid metals drives the dispersion of active atoms in liquid metals at elevated temperatures. These dynamically migrating single atoms can be subsequently combined with liquid metal, profiting from its good metallic affinity and forming a stable interaction between these two kinds of atoms. In light of this, equipped with the naturally metallic affinity and fluidity of liquid metal, the highly thermal-stable SACs can be realized.

The liquid metal dispersed SACs are synthesized by dissolving Pt nanoparticles into liquid Ga at elevated temperatures. The mechanism illustrating the formation process of the liquid metal dispersed SACs is shown in Fig. 1a. Firstly, the Pt particles were sprinkled evenly over the liquid metal. As the temperature gradually increases, the solubility of the active metal in the dispersion is further increased, and the active metal can efficiently disperse in the liquid metal within its limited solubility. The Pt−Pt bonds in the original Pt metal nanoparticles are broken and tend to bind tightly to Ga atoms and form a thermodynamically stable configuration with Ga atoms, benefiting from the good affinity between Ga and Pt. The stable Pt−Ga interaction curtails the sintering of Pt single atoms. Moreover, according to the Arrhenius equation25, the thermal motion of atoms would be intensified by high temperature, promoting the rapid diffusion between Pt and Ga atoms and the continuous renewal of Pt single atoms exposed on the catalytic surface (Fig. 1b). In contrast, when single atoms are anchored to solid supports, their co-migration with the supports becomes kinetically constrained. Once the metal-support interactions become insufficient to compensate for the inherently high surface energy of single atoms, these atoms tend to detach from the solid supports and aggregate. This process is exothermic, where minimization of total surface energy governs particle growth26. Meanwhile, some single atoms may embed into the lattice of supports, becoming buried when the interaction between the support and metal atoms is too strong. These lead to the loss of active sites, reducing the stability of SACs and consequently affecting their activity and selectivity (Fig. 1c).

Thermal stability of active metal atoms mono-dispersed in liquid Ga

Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were employed to elucidate the atomic-scale dispersed state of active metal in liquid metal (computational details are provided in the supplementary information). Using Pt as a model of Pt cluster, we investigated the structural evolution of both clustered and dispersed Pt in liquid Ga during 10 ps simulations at 923 K (Figs. 2a, b and Supplementary Movs. 1, 2). The calculated total energy versus time curves for the Ga Pt system containing clustered Pt and dispersed Pt (Fig. 2c) reveal that the dispersed Pt generally exhibits lower total energy compared to the aggregated Pt clusters within the simulated 10 ps. The results indicate that the remarkable atomic diffusion of liquid Ga metal at high temperature promotes the migration of heterogeneous active metal atoms, thereby stabilizing their dispersed atomic state in liquid Ga.

The relatively high Pt concentration in the Ga Pt system leads to intermittent formation of Pt dimer, as evidenced by the time-dependent curve of the shortest Pt–Pt distance (Supplementary Fig. 1). To further elucidate the actual existence state of Pt atoms in liquid Ga, we performed AIMD simulations of the Ga Pt system (a Pt dimer embedded in Ga ) at 923 K. The 10 ps NVT ensemble simulations (Fig. 2d) display that the Pt–Pt interatomic distance progressively increases from 4.18 Å to 11.63 Å, significantly exceeding the Pt–Pt bond length of 2.65 ~ 2.79 Å28. This unequivocally confirms that Pt atoms preferentially exist as monatomic species in the liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Movs. 3, 4). Further statistical analysis of the coordination environment of Pt atoms in the Ga Pt system shows that the dominant coordination numbers for individual Pt atoms are 8 or 9 (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4), implying that mono-dispersed Pt atoms migrate within liquid Ga in the form of clusters such as Ga Pt or Ga Pt (Supplementary Fig. 5).

To fundamentally understand the thermodynamic preference for Pt mono-dispersion in liquid Ga, we systematically calculated the bond energy difference ∆E (∆𝐸 = 𝐸 + 𝐸̅ −2𝐸 ) only for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Figs. 6 ~ 11). Here, 𝐸̅ represents the average Ga–Ga bond energy in the Ga molecular clusters, 𝐸 denotes the Pt–Pt bond energy in the (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, and 𝐸 refers to the Ga–Pt bond energy in the Ga Pt molecular clusters. The results indicate that the ∆E values for the Pt , (Ga Pt) , (Ga Pt) , and (Ga Pt) molecular clusters, evaluated using different computational methods (B3LYP, MN15L, and M06L), are all greater than zero. This demonstrates that in these molecular systems, the Ga atoms involved in bond-breaking readily disrupt the Pt–Pt bonds, leading to the formation of stable Pt–Ga–Pt bridging units, thereby promoting the single-atom dispersion of Pt in liquid Ga. Meanwhile, we calculated the formation energies of Pt Ga, (Ga Pt) Ga, and (Ga Pt) Ga molecules, which were determined to be 101.1, 46.2, and 57.9 kcal mol–1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12 and Fig. 2f). Additionally, we roughly estimated the energy barriers of Ga atom insertion into the Pt–Pt bond to be 58.2, 13.4, and 40.2 kcal mol–1 by performing rigid scans of the Pt–Ga–Pt angle (Supplementary Fig. 13 and Fig. 2f). These results clearly demonstrate that, both thermodynamically and kinetically, Ga atoms in liquid Ga at 923 K can readily disrupt Pt–Pt bonds, thereby promoting the mono-dispersion of Pt atoms.

To more intuitively demonstrate the mono-dispersion state of Pt atoms in Ga, we constructed Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures with Pt contents of 2 at% and 0.2 at%, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 14). Meanwhile, based on a training dataset containing 17347 structures and a test dataset of 1926 structures, we trained a Ga–Pt neuroevolution potential model (Supplementary Fig. 15). The consistency between the calculated and experimental solubility validates the effectiveness of the constructed machine learning force field in evaluating the dissolution of Pt in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 16). Subsequently, we performed 20 ns NVT molecular dynamics simulations at 923 K on the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures using the trained Ga–Pt machine-learning potential. The simulation results clearly indicate that the Pt cluster rapidly disperse in liquid Ga (Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, we analyzed the proportions of mono-dispersed and dimerized Pt states in all structures over the last 10 ns (Fig. 2g). In the Ga Pt structure, the proportion of mono-dispersed Pt was 98.2%, while in the Ga Pt structure, it reached 99.9%. The results clearly demonstrate that in structures with Pt content of 2 at% or below, Pt atoms can be considered fully mono-dispersed at 923 K. Moreover, the calculated average numbers of surface atoms in the Ga Pt and Ga Pt structures are 5.4 and 3.0, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 18 and Supplementary Fig. 19), and the temporal evolution of the vertical migration of individual Pt atoms and their probability distribution demonstrate a preferential tendency to migrate toward the surface (Supplementary Fig. 20). These indicate that a certain proportion of mono-dispersed Pt atoms can continuously exist on the liquid surface and participate in relevant catalytic reactions. Overall, the stable Ga Pt and similar clusters that are formed profited from the favorable affinity between Ga and Pt inhibit the aggregation and sintering of Pt during thermal motion, laying the foundation for synthesizing the highly thermal-stable SACs.

Characterization of liquid catalyst

To further validate that liquid metal can act as the dispersion for single atoms, we synthesized the Ga-dispersed Pt SACs (Pt SACs@Ga). The detailed structure of the catalyst was characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The Pt species in the liquid metal exists in a mono-disperse distribution without the obvious occurrence of aggregated Pt (Fig. 3a). The bright-field image of Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst maintains an almost invariant brightness across the whole particle and the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) data shows no diffraction spots of Pt in the amorphous ring, revealing the lack of long-range order structure in the Ga–Pt catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 21 and Fig. 3b). Furthermore, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum was employed to reveal the chemical composition and electronic structure of the liquid metal dispersed SACs. Before the execution of XPS measurements, the sample underwent etching with argon ions to eliminate the natural oxide layer and surface contaminants. Ga 2p peaks appear at 1116.73 eV and 1116.59 eV (Fig. 3c), which are consistent with the reported binding energies of metallic Ga (Ga0 2p =1116.70 eV). Meanwhile, due to the higher electronegativity of Pt (2.28) than that of Ga (1.81)29, the Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga system served as the electron acceptor, and the Pt 4f and 4f peaks in Pt SACs@Ga exhibit a positive shift (1.0 eV) than those in pure Pt metal (Fig. 3d). It is a consensus that metallic Pt0 species occupy a preeminent role as the active sites for many catalytic processes30–32. This guarantees a proficient and robust distribution of single atoms while preserving their catalytic activity. Furthermore, the absence of the obvious aggregation of Pt atoms in the Pt SACs@Ga is further identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) tests, where no signal of Pt (PDF#04-0802) is observed (Supplementary Fig. 22). To mitigate the potential inaccuracies arising from the insensitivity of XRD to small Pt clusters, the pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was conducted to delve into the interatomic structure of the Pt SACs@Ga liquid catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 23). The absence of Pt–Pt bonds indicates that Pt is distributed nearly at the atomic level within the liquid Ga without the formation of Pt clusters. These observations suggest that liquid metal can achieve the efficient uniform dispersion of highly active single atoms at elevated temperatures.

To further verify the exact dispersion state of Pt in the Pt SACs@Ga catalyst, X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were conducted. The X-ray absorption edge near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum shows that the intensity of the white line at the L edge of Pt lies between that of the Pt foil and that of PtO . Correspondingly, the k -weighted R-space Fourier transformed spectra of the extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectra (EXAFS) show the prominent peak at 2.14 Å for Pt SACs@Ga distinguished from that of the Pt–O (1.62 Å) bonds for PtO and the Pt–Pt bonds (2.24 Å) for Pt foil (Fig. 3f). All these results intuitively indicate that the Pt exists in the single-atom state in liquid metal.

EDH performance of liquid metal dispersed SACs

Based on the computational results, the liquid metal dispersed SACSs theoretically feature excellent thermal stability at high temperatures. It is necessary to conduct specific high-temperature tests for verification. Pt-based catalysts are used for the dehydrogenation of alkanes due to their high efficiency in activating the C−H bonds of alkanes and low propensity in breaking C−C bonds33,34. And Pt−Sn/Al O (Oleflex process) is the primary industrial technology operated for direct propane dehydrogenation35. While it suffers from severe sintering and coke, which results in rapid deactivation and restricts the selectivity36. Therefore, as a proof of concept, the thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs was validated by EDH. As shown in Fig. 4a, when exposed to ethane, Pt single atoms exposed on the surface capture ethane molecules and synergistically activate C–H bonds, leading to selective EDH to ethylene. Meanwhile, the fluidic characteristic of liquid metal dispersed SACs at operating conditions enables continuous replenishment of catalytically active Pt atoms onto the surface. The stable interaction between Pt−Ga effectively blocks the aggregation of Pt atoms during the constant migration. Benefiting from the advantages mentioned above, these adaptive surface active sites maintain long-term activity and thermal stability.

To circumvent the issue of inadequate interaction between the liquid metal dispersed SACs and the reaction gas, the porous support is utilized to amplify the gas mass transfer rate. So, we coupled liquid metal dispersed SACs with porous MFI zeolite (ZSM-5) by the physical approach of ultrasonication to increase the contact surface area between the liquid metal support SACs and gas reactants. As demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 24, EDS mappings revealed a well-distribution of Ga, Si, and Al, indicating the liquid metal is uniformly loaded in the ZSM-5 zeolite framework. Upon heating, Pt will be spontaneously dispersed in Ga homogeneously, achieving the preparation of a zeolite-dispersed liquid metal supported SACs (Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5). Further, we performed in situ XRD to explore the dispersing process of Pt (Supplementary Fig. 25). The diffraction peak observed at 43 ~ 47o originates from the carbon in situ reactor (Supplementary Fig. 26). Initially, the characteristic peaks of Pt can be apparently observed, which are located at 39.76o and 46.24o. With the temperature increasing, the characteristic peaks of Pt were gradually weakened and disappeared subsequently, proving the dispersion of Pt particles.

The catalytic performance was evaluated in non-oxidative EDH at 923 K in a fixed-bed quartz U-tube reactor under atmospheric pressure with a feed gas of 12.5 vol% C H in Ar. The Pt particles/ZSM-5 catalyst, which is synthesized by direct mixing commercial Pt particles with ZSM-5, exhibits ethane conversion at 9.5% and ethylene selectivity at 82.6% (Figs. 4b, c). Interestingly, the liquid metal dispersed SACs are highly active with ethane conversion at 17.8% and ethylene selectivity at 98.3%. This is because the introduction of liquid metal alters the state of Pt. By dispersing Pt particles into single Pt atoms, the utilization of Pt atoms is maximized to achieve high conversion rates. Furthermore, since the size of Pt particle significantly influences catalytic performance, larger Pt nanoparticles typically promote C−C cleavage and deep dehydrogenation side reactions37. In contrast, Pt-based catalysts dispersed at the atomic scale exhibit excellent selectivity for ethylene due to their superior activation of C−H bonds in alkanes, while simultaneously limiting C−C bond cleavage to prevent dehydrogenation reactions. Therefore, when liquid metal is introduced, Pt exists in a single-atom state, enabling the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst to achieve high selectivity. To verify the universality of the strategy that liquid metals can disperse metals into single atoms, we extended the synthesis approach to other systems and successfully synthesized liquid metal dispersed Rh SACs (Supplementary Fig. 27). Moreover, Rh SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 exhibits significantly improved catalytic performance compared to Rh particles/ZSM-5 in EDH (Supplementary Fig. 28).

To gain a deeper understanding of the effects of liquid metal dispersed SACs and nano catalysts on the dehydrogenation reaction of ethane, we conducted kinetic studies on both types of catalysts. We measured the ethane conversion in a temperature range of 883 ~ 933 K and fitted the data according to the Arrhenius equation to calculate the apparent activation energy for EDH. The apparent activation energies for Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 and Pt particles/ZSM-5 are 102.44 kJ mol−1 and 137.18 kJ mol−1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 29). The significantly reduced activation energy indicates a decreased energy barrier that needs to be overcome for the reaction to proceed. And the single Pt atom dispersed in the liquid Ga can more effectively weaken the C–H bond of ethane than Pt particles. Therefore, the Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibits superior catalytic performance.

The performance of the liquid metal dispersed SACs in the durability test is presented in Fig. 4d. It exhibits sustainable conversion and selectivity in the continuous reaction for 100 h, where the constant ethane conversion of ~18% is obtained without attenuation. And liquid metal dispersed SACs exhibit a steady ethene productivity of around 14.3 g g −1 h−1 during the 100 h Pt EDH test. The catalyst displays no deactivation trend during the testing period, indicating a reasonable expectation of more durable stability. Notably, the XANES spectrum and R-space of liquid metal dispersed SACs after 100 h EDH at Pt L -edge are similar to those of pristine liquid SACs (Figs. 4e, f and Figs. 3e, f), demonstrating exceptional structural integrity under prolonged thermal catalysis. The catalytic performance and structural characterization together confirmed the superior thermal stability of liquid metal dispersed SACs in extremely high temperatures, which remarkably outperforms the traditional solid support loaded SACs. To further substantiate the thermal stability performance of our work, comparing the catalytic reaction temperatures and time on stream of Pt SACs@Ga/ZSM-5 with reported SACs (Supplementary Tab. 1), where the results remain outstanding. The excellent stability, selectivity, and conversion indicate the potential of liquid metal dispersed SACs for reactions limited in harsh conditions.
