Comment 2: The mechanism of high temperature stability is not clear. The authors need
to prepare a single Pt atom in molten Ga, and Pt almost remain the top of the molten Ga
cluster and also high temperature stability.
Author Reply: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Following your suggestion, the
stability mechanism of Pt single atom on Ga was demonstrated through the theoretical
calculations. We constructed the simulation model, in which the atom ratio and temperature
are strictly consistent with those in the experiment. The results confirmed the single-atom
dispersion state of Pt atoms in liquid metal, consistent with the experimental findings.
1) Theoretical calculations have proved that a single Pt atom in molten Ga can
freely migrate in the molten Ga, and there is a certain probability for it being exposed
on the Ga surface. To validate this mechanism, we constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁ slab model. AIMD
simulations were conducted to investigate the motion trajectory of a single Pt atom in molten
Ga (analyzing its vertical distance to the surface). Throughout the 10 ps simulation period,
a single Pt atom migrates relatively freely within molten Ga, with a depth from the Ga
surface ranging from 0 to 4.84 Å (Fig. R7). Statistical analysis indicates a surface exposure
probability of 56.3% for the isolated Pt atom. Furthermore, considering the susceptibility of
metallic Ga to oxidation state, even under reducing atmospheres (e.g., H₂) at 923 K, a thin
Ga₂O₃ layer may persist. To eliminate the influence of Ga oxidation on Pt exposure, we also
constructed a Ga₇₉Pt₁O₁₀ slab model incorporating a small number of oxygen atoms and
performed a 10 ps AIMD simulation. The simulation results demonstrate that limited
oxygen atoms form Ga₂O₃ clusters with surface Ga atoms. Under the influence of these
Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga surface, the Pt atom primarily remains within the surface
and subsurface regions, exhibiting a depth range of 0 to 2.97 Å (Fig. R10). Notably, the
surface exposure probability of the single Pt atom increases significantly to 81.3%. The
single Pt atom in liquid metal migrates freely as Ga₈Pt or Ga₉Pt clusters, retaining a finite
probability of surface exposure. Crucially, the presence of Ga₂O₃ clusters at the molten Ga
surface dramatically enhances the probability of single Pt atom surface exposure. This
indicates that the Pt single atom can be stabilized to the molten Ga surface at 923 K
over extended periods, thereby serving as active sites for the catalytic activation of
C₂H₆ molecules.
Fig. R10 | The distance between a single Pt atom and the surface Ga layer. a The calculated curve of
the distance between a single Pt atom and the surface Ga layer as a function of time. b The illustration
of the distance between a single Pt atom and the surface Ga layer. Here, surface Ga atoms are
characterized as top-layer Ga atoms in each frame structure whose coordination number is two less than
the maximum coordination number, with the zero point in the z-direction defined as the average of the
maximum and minimum z-coordinates of these surface Ga atoms. Furthermore, the z-coordinate
threshold for identifying exposed Pt atoms is defined as the vertical distance corresponding to the closest
packing radius of Re atoms relative to this zero reference point.
2) The mechanism of high temperature stability stems from the stable interaction
between Pt and Ga, which is validated by both thermodynamics and dynamics. Firstly,
thermodynamic analysis reveals that the system exhibits a lower total energy for Pt
monodispersed in liquid metal than as clusters (Fig. R11a). Therefore, the remarkable
atomic diffusion of liquid Ga metal at high temperature promotes the migration of
heterogeneous active metal atoms, thereby stabilizing their dispersed atomic state in liquid
Ga rather than forming dimers and trimers inside the molten Ga. Secondly, dynamic
simulations of Pt atoms diffusion within Ga demonstrate that Pt atoms are resistant to
aggregation. The Pt–Pt interatomic distance progressively increases from 4.18 Å to 11.63 Å
(Fig. R11b), significantly exceeding the typical Pt–Pt bond length range of 2.65–2.79 Å (J.
Am. Chem. Soc. 1978, 100, 2074). All these results confirm that Pt atoms maintain stable
single-atom states under high temperature.

4) The long-term stability test of liquid metal dispersed SACs further verified the
stability of the atomically dispersed configuration. During the catalytic process, the state
of the active center directly affects the catalytic pathway. Usually, the formation of Pt
particles leads to deep dehydrogenation of alkanes, resulting in a decrease in the selectivity
and conversion of the catalyst. In our work, the performance of the liquid metal dispersed
SACs in the durability test exhibits sustainable conversion and selectivity in the continuous
reaction for 100 h, where the constant ethane conversion of ~18% is obtained without
attenuation (Fig. R16). These results provide indirect evidence that the catalyst maintains a
